title: World Geography
summary: Solar system, Earth's motions and time, interior and rocks, atmosphere and winds, oceans and currents, continental superlatives and boundary lines. CGL usually asks one question here — local winds, planets, straits and 'largest/longest' facts dominate.

subtopics.title: Solar system, Earth's motions, latitudes and time
subtopics.concept:
### Solar system (8 planets since the IAU decision of 2006, when Pluto became a **dwarf planet**)
Order from the Sun: **Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune** ('My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Noodles').

| Planet | Remember it as |
|---|---|
| **Mercury** | Smallest planet, nearest to the Sun, fastest orbit |
| **Venus** | **Hottest** planet (thick CO₂ atmosphere), brightest, 'Earth's twin', **morning/evening star**, rotates **east to west** (retrograde) |
| **Earth** | 'Blue planet'; only known planet with life |
| **Mars** | '**Red planet**' (iron oxide); Olympus Mons; moons **Phobos and Deimos** |
| **Jupiter** | **Largest** planet; Great Red Spot; **Ganymede** — largest moon of the solar system |
| **Saturn** | Prominent **rings**; **least dense** (lighter than water); largest moon **Titan** |
| **Uranus** | Rotates **on its side** (extreme axial tilt); also retrograde spin |
| **Neptune** | Farthest planet; strongest winds |

Sunlight takes about **8 minutes 20 seconds** to reach the Earth. The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite; the same face always points towards Earth.

### Motions of the Earth
| Motion | Period | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| **Rotation** (west to east) | About 24 hours (sidereal day 23 h 56 m 4 s) | Day and night |
| **Revolution** | About 365¼ days | Seasons (with the tilt) |

- Axis is tilted **23½°** from the perpendicular (makes **66½°** with the orbital plane).
- **Perihelion** (nearest to Sun) about **3 January**; **aphelion** (farthest) about **4 July**.
- **Summer solstice 21 June** — longest day in the Northern Hemisphere, Sun overhead at the Tropic of Cancer. **Winter solstice 22 December** — Sun over the Tropic of Capricorn.
- **Equinoxes — 21 March and 23 September** — Sun overhead at the equator; day = night everywhere.

### Latitudes, longitudes and time
| Line | Value |
|---|---|
| Equator | 0° (longest parallel, a great circle) |
| Tropic of Cancer / Capricorn | 23½° N / 23½° S |
| Arctic / Antarctic Circle | 66½° N / 66½° S |
| Prime Meridian | 0° through **Greenwich** (London) |
| **International Date Line** | Roughly **180°**, zig-zags to avoid land |

- Earth turns 360° in 24 hours → **15° = 1 hour**, **1° = 4 minutes**.
- Places **east** of Greenwich are **ahead** in time; places west are behind.
- Crossing the IDL **westward** (e.g. USA → Japan) you **add a day**; crossing **eastward** you repeat a day.

tricks.title: Planet superlatives in one line
tricks.body: **Mercury** smallest–nearest, **Venus** hottest–brightest–backward spin, **Mars** red, **Jupiter** largest (Ganymede biggest moon), **Saturn** rings–lightest, **Uranus** on its side, **Neptune** farthest–windiest.

example.q: Which is the hottest planet?
example.solution: Venus — not Mercury — because its thick CO₂ atmosphere traps heat.

tricks.title: IST from the meridian
tricks.body: India's meridian is 82½°E → 82.5 × 4 = 330 minutes = **5 h 30 min ahead of GMT**.

example.q: When it is 12 noon at Greenwich, what is the time at 90°E?

mistakes: Calling Mercury the hottest planet — Venus is hotter despite being farther.
Adding time for places west of Greenwich — west is behind, east is ahead.
Mixing perihelion (January) with summer in the Northern Hemisphere — seasons come from the tilt, not distance.
subtopics.notes:
### The universe, the Sun and the solar system
The universe is made of **galaxies**; ours is the **Milky Way** (Akash Ganga). A **light year** is the distance light covers in one year - about **9.46 x 10^12 km** - so it measures distance, not time. The **Sun**, our nearest star, is about **150 million km (8 light-minutes)** away; the next star is **Proxima Centauri**. The **solar system** holds the Sun, **8 planets**, their moons, asteroids and comets. In **2006** the IAU made **Pluto** a **dwarf planet**, taking the planets from 9 to 8.

### The eight planets - the exam one-liners
| Planet | Key facts |
|---|---|
| **Mercury** | Smallest, nearest to the Sun, no atmosphere or moon; extreme day-night temperatures |
| **Venus** | **Hottest** planet (thick CO2 greenhouse); brightest; the **Morning/Evening Star**; 'Earth's twin' in size; rotates **east to west** |
| **Earth** | The **Blue Planet** - about 71% water; only known planet with life |
| **Mars** | The **Red Planet** (iron-oxide dust); **Olympus Mons**, the solar system's largest volcano; moons **Phobos and Deimos** |
| **Jupiter** | **Largest** planet; **Great Red Spot** storm; its moon **Ganymede** is the solar system's **largest satellite** |
| **Saturn** | Famous **rings** of ice and rock; **least dense** planet; moon **Titan** is the second largest satellite |
| **Uranus** | 'Ice giant'; axis so tilted that it seems to **roll on its side**; discovered in 1781 by William Herschel |
| **Neptune** | Farthest planet; deepest blue; the strongest winds of the solar system |

**Order from the Sun:** Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars - the small rocky **inner (terrestrial) planets**; then the **asteroid belt**; then Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune - the large gas **outer (Jovian) planets**. The largest asteroid **Ceres** lies in this belt. **Comets** (e.g. **Halley's**, seen every **76 years** - last 1986, next 2061) grow tails that always point **away from the Sun**. **Meteors** ('shooting stars') burn up in the air; the ones that reach the ground are **meteorites**.

### The Earth's size, shape and the Moon
Earth is an **oblate spheroid (geoid)** - flattened at the poles, bulging at the equator: equatorial diameter about **12,756 km**, polar **12,714 km**, equatorial circumference about **40,075 km**. Its only natural satellite, the **Moon**, is about **3.84 lakh km** away; it **rotates on its axis in the same time (about 27.3 days) as it takes to revolve** around Earth, so we always see the same face. It has practically **no atmosphere**, so astronauts' footprints stay; **Neil Armstrong** stepped on it on **20 July 1969** (Apollo 11), with Buzz Aldrin.

### Rotation, revolution and the seasons
- **Rotation** - Earth spins west to east once in **23 h 56 min 4 s** (the sidereal day), causing **day and night** and wind deflection (Coriolis effect).
- **Revolution** - Earth goes round the Sun in **365 days 6 hours 9 minutes**; the extra 6 hours is adjusted by **29 February every 4th (leap) year**. Revolution plus the tilted axis (23.5 degrees) causes the **seasons**.
- On **3 January** Earth is nearest the Sun (**perihelion**); on **4 July** farthest (**aphelion**).

### Equinoxes and solstices
| Date | Event | Effect in the Northern Hemisphere |
|---|---|---|
| **21 March** | Vernal (spring) equinox | Day = night everywhere |
| **21 June** | Summer solstice | **Longest day**; Sun overhead the **Tropic of Cancer** |
| **23 September** | Autumnal equinox | Day = night everywhere |
| **22 December** | Winter solstice | **Shortest day**; Sun overhead the **Tropic of Capricorn** |

On the **equator**, day and night stay about equal all year; beyond the Arctic/Antarctic Circles (66.5 degrees), summer brings months-long days - the 'land of the midnight sun'.

### Latitudes, longitudes and time
**Latitudes** are 180 imaginary circles (90 N + 90 S) measured from the **equator**; the important ones are the Equator (0), Tropics (23.5 N/S) and Circles (66.5 N/S). **Longitudes** are 360 meridians joining the poles; **1 degree = 4 minutes of time**. The **Prime Meridian (0 degrees, Greenwich)** was fixed at the 1884 conference; places east are ahead in time, west behind. India keeps **IST = GMT + 5 h 30 min** (meridian 82.5 E). The **International Date Line** (IDL) follows roughly the 180th meridian, bending around islands; crossing it **east to west (towards Asia) you ADD a day**, west to east you LOSE a day.

### Quick revision
- 8 planets (Pluto = dwarf planet since 2006); order M-V-E-M (asteroid belt) J-S-U-N.
- Venus hottest + Morning/Evening star; Jupiter largest + Ganymede biggest moon; Saturn least dense; Mars red + Olympus Mons.
- Light year = distance unit; the Sun is 8 light-minutes away.
- Rotation 23 h 56 m 4 s (day-night); revolution 365 d 6 h (seasons, leap year).
- 21 June summer solstice (Sun on Tropic of Cancer); 22 Dec winter solstice; 21 Mar & 23 Sep equinoxes.
- 1 degree longitude = 4 minutes; IDL: east to west = add a day; west to east = lose a day.

patterns.name: Planet superlatives and pairs
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is the largest/hottest/brightest planet?', 'Earth's twin', 'red planet', 'planet with rings', planet-property match-the-column.
patterns.logic:
1. Size ladder: Jupiter > Saturn > Uranus > Neptune > Earth > Venus > Mars > Mercury.
2. Venus - hottest, brightest, Morning/Evening Star, 'Earth's twin', rotates east to west; Mars - red planet with Olympus Mons; Saturn - rings, least dense.
3. For match-the-column, fix one anchor per planet and eliminate; 'largest satellite' (Ganymede) belongs to Jupiter, second largest (Titan) to Saturn.

example.q: Which planet is known as the 'Earth's twin' because of its similar size and mass?
example.solution: **Venus**. It is also the hottest planet (thick CO2) and the brightest, called the Morning/Evening Star.

patterns.name: The Moon: distance, motions and landings
patterns.howToSpot: 'How far is the Moon', 'why does the Moon always show the same face', first man on the Moon, the Moon's atmosphere.
patterns.logic:
1. Distance about **3.84 lakh km**; the Moon is Earth's only natural satellite.
2. Its **rotation period equals its revolution period (about 27.3 days)** - hence the same face always faces Earth.
3. It has practically **no atmosphere**; Neil Armstrong stepped on it on **20 July 1969** (Apollo 11).

example.q: Why do we always see the same face of the Moon?
example.solution: Because the Moon's **rotation on its axis takes the same time (about 27.3 days) as its revolution** around the Earth.

patterns.name: Equinoxes, solstices and the overhead Sun
patterns.howToSpot: 'Longest/shortest day', 'the Sun is overhead the Tropic of Cancer on', 'when is day and night equal', dates with hemisphere effects.
patterns.logic:
1. Solstices: **21 June** (longest day in the N. Hemisphere; Sun overhead Tropic of Cancer) and **22 December** (shortest day; Sun overhead Tropic of Capricorn).
2. Equinoxes: **21 March** and **23 September** - day and night equal everywhere.
3. The hemisphere rule: what is summer in the north is winter in the south; on the equator days stay about 12 hours.

example.q: On which date is the Sun vertically overhead the Tropic of Capricorn?
example.solution: **22 December** - the winter solstice of the Northern Hemisphere (its shortest day) and the height of summer in the south.

patterns.name: Rotation vs revolution and their effects
patterns.howToSpot: 'Rotation causes', 'length of the sidereal day', 'why a leap year', perihelion and aphelion dates.
patterns.logic:
1. **Rotation** (once in 23 h 56 min 4 s) causes day-night, the Sun's apparent eastward rise, tides (partly) and wind deflection.
2. **Revolution** (365 d 6 h 9 min) with the 23.5-degree tilt causes the **seasons**; the extra 6 h gives a leap year every 4 years.
3. Perihelion (nearest Sun) - **3 January**; aphelion (farthest) - **4 July**. In questions, separate 'day and night' (rotation) from 'seasons' (revolution).

example.q: Why is a leap year observed every fourth year?
example.solution: The Earth takes **365 days 6 hours 9 minutes** to revolve; the leftover 6 hours collects into one extra day (29 February) every four years.

patterns.name: Longitudes, time zones and the IDL
patterns.howToSpot: Time difference between two longitudes, IST-GMT relation, adding/losing a day across the IDL, count of latitudes/meridians.
patterns.logic:
1. The Earth turns 360 degrees in 24 hours, so **1 degree = 4 minutes**; 15 degrees = 1 hour.
2. East of Greenwich is ahead, west behind; IST is based on 82.5 E = **GMT + 5 h 30 min**.
3. The **IDL** follows about 180 degrees: crossing **east to west (towards Asia) add a day**, west to east lose a day.

example.q: Two places lie 30 degrees of longitude apart. What is the difference in their local time?
example.solution: 30 x 4 minutes = **120 minutes = 2 hours**; the eastern place is ahead.

subtopics.title: Earth's interior, earthquakes, rocks and volcanoes
subtopics.concept:
### Interior of the Earth
| Layer | Nature | Old name |
|---|---|---|
| **Crust** | Thinnest; continental crust mostly silica + aluminium | **SiAl** |
| **Mantle** | Silica + magnesium; upper part includes the **asthenosphere** (magma source) | **SiMa** |
| **Core** | Nickel + iron; **outer core liquid**, **inner core solid** | **NiFe** |

Discontinuities: **Conrad** (within crust), **Mohorovičić / Moho** (crust–mantle), **Gutenberg** (mantle–core), **Lehmann** (outer–inner core).

### Earthquakes
- Point of origin inside the Earth = **focus (hypocentre)**; point on the surface directly above = **epicentre**.
- **P-waves** (primary) are fastest and travel through solids, liquids and gases. **S-waves** (secondary) cannot pass through liquids — their **shadow zone** proved the outer core is liquid. **Surface (L) waves** are slowest and most destructive.
- Recorded by a **seismograph**; **Richter scale** measures **magnitude** (energy, logarithmic), **Mercalli scale** measures **intensity** (damage).

### Rocks
| Type | Formed by | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Igneous** ('primary rocks') | Cooling of magma/lava | **Granite** (intrusive), **basalt** (extrusive) |
| **Sedimentary** | Layers of deposits; contain **fossils** | Sandstone, shale, **limestone**, coal |
| **Metamorphic** | Heat and pressure change existing rocks | **Limestone → marble**, **sandstone → quartzite**, **shale → slate**, **granite → gneiss** |

### Volcanoes and plates
- About two-thirds of active volcanoes lie on the **Pacific 'Ring of Fire'**.
- **Stromboli** (Italy) is the 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean'; **Vesuvius** buried Pompeii in AD 79; **Krakatoa** (Indonesia) erupted catastrophically in 1883; **Mauna Loa** (Hawaii) is the largest active volcano.
- **Fold mountains** (Himalayas, Alps, Andes, Rockies) form at **convergent** plate boundaries; **mid-ocean ridges** form at divergent boundaries; the **San Andreas Fault** is a transform boundary.
- **Continental drift** was proposed by **Alfred Wegener** (1912); the supercontinent was **Pangaea**, surrounded by the ocean **Panthalassa**.

example.q: Which discontinuity separates the crust from the mantle?
example.solution: The Mohorovičić (Moho) discontinuity.

tricks.title: Metamorphic pairs: 'Lime-Marble, Sand-Quartz, Shale-Slate, Granite-Gneiss'
tricks.body: The first letters of the new rock are easy: **M**arble from **L**imestone is the most asked (Taj Mahal marble).

mistakes: Saying S-waves travel through the outer core — they cannot pass through liquids.
Calling granite a sedimentary rock — it is an intrusive igneous rock.
subtopics.notes:
### Inside the Earth - three layers
Our knowledge of the interior comes from **seismic waves** and mining, not direct observation. The three layers:
| Layer | Depth (about) | Key facts |
|---|---|---|
| **Crust** | 5-10 km (ocean floors) to 30-70 km (continents) | Thinnest layer; continental crust = **SiAl** (silica + aluminium), lighter; oceanic = **SiMa** (silica + magnesium), denser |
| **Mantle** | up to about 2,900 km | Mostly solid rock; the partly-molten **asthenosphere** in its upper part is the source of magma |
| **Core** | 2,900 km to centre (6,371 km) | **NiFe** - nickel and iron; **outer core liquid**, **inner core solid** |

**Discontinuities** (surfaces where wave speeds jump) - remember the order top to bottom: **Conrad** (within the crust), **Mohorovicic (Moho)** - crust and mantle (1909), **Repetti** (within the mantle), **Gutenberg** - mantle and outer core (about 2,900 km), **Lehmann** - outer and inner core.

### Earthquakes
An **earthquake** is a sudden shake caused by the release of stored energy along faults. The point inside the Earth where it starts is the **focus (hypocentre)**; the point on the surface directly above is the **epicentre** (shock strongest there). Waves are recorded by a **seismograph**.
- **P-waves (primary)** - fastest, longitudinal, pass through solids **and liquids**.
- **S-waves (secondary)** - slower, transverse, **cannot pass through liquids** - this proves the outer core is liquid.
- **L-waves (surface)** - slowest, arrive last, do the **most damage**.
Magnitude is measured on the **Richter scale**; damage (intensity) on the **Mercalli scale**. About **80% of the world's earthquakes** occur in the **Circum-Pacific belt - the 'Ring of Fire'**. Giant sea waves set off by undersea earthquakes are **tsunamis** (a Japanese word meaning 'harbour wave'), as in the Indian Ocean tsunami of 2004.

### Volcanoes
A volcano is an opening where magma (molten rock), ash and gases escape.
- By activity: **active** (Barren Island - **India's only active volcano**; Stromboli, the 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean'; Etna; Vesuvius, which buried Pompeii in 79 AD), **dormant** (sleeping, e.g. Fuji) and **extinct** (no record of eruption).
- By shape: **shield** volcanoes (broad, runny lava - Mauna Loa, Hawaii), **composite (strato) volcanoes** (steep, alternating lava and ash - Fuji, Vesuvius), and **calderas** (collapsed craters).
- Hot springs and **geysers** (e.g. Old Faithful of Yellowstone, USA) are related features. Volcanoes also cluster in the Ring of Fire and along mid-ocean ridges.

### Rocks - three families
| Family | Formed by | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Igneous** | Cooling of magma/lava ('fire rocks'; the oldest, primary rocks) | **Granite** (intrusive/plutonic, big crystals), **basalt** (extrusive/volcanic; ocean floors) |
| **Sedimentary** | Layers (strata) of sediments pressed together; **the only rocks with fossils**; cover most of the land surface | Sandstone, shale, limestone, coal |
| **Metamorphic** | Heat + pressure change an existing rock | Limestone to **marble**, sandstone to **quartzite**, shale to **slate**, granite to **gneiss** |

The endless conversion of one rock type into another is the **rock cycle**. Igneous and metamorphic rocks hold most minerals (gold, copper); coal, oil and limestone - the economic favourites - sit in sedimentary rocks.

### Mountains, plateaus and plains - the big division
- **Fold mountains** - crust squeezed into folds by plate collision; the **young fold mountains** (Himalayas, Alps, Andes, Rockies) are the highest; older folds (Aravallis, Urals) are worn down.
- **Block mountains** - land raised between two faults (Vosges, Black Forest, Sierra Nevada); **rift valleys** (Rhine, East Africa) are the sunken blocks between faults.
- **Volcanic mountains** - built by eruptions (Fuji, Kilimanjaro).
- **Plateaus** - raised flatlands (Tibet, the highest and largest; Deccan); **plains** - low, flat, fertile, the most densely populated landforms.

### Quick revision
- Layers: crust (SiAl/SiMa) - mantle - core (NiFe); outer core liquid, inner solid.
- Discontinuity order 'Come Make Good Lunch': Conrad, Moho, Repetti, Gutenberg, Lehmann.
- S-waves stop at liquid - proof the outer core is molten; Richter = magnitude, Mercalli = intensity.
- 80% of earthquakes and volcanoes: Pacific **Ring of Fire**; Barren Island = India's only active volcano.
- Igneous (granite, basalt), sedimentary (fossils: limestone, coal), metamorphic (marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss).
- Young fold mountains: Himalaya, Alps, Andes, Rockies; Tibet = highest plateau.

patterns.name: Layers of the Earth and discontinuities
patterns.howToSpot: 'The boundary between crust and mantle is', 'which layer is made of nickel and iron', 'SiAl/SiMa/NiFe', ordering of Conrad-Moho-Repetti-Gutenberg-Lehmann.
patterns.logic:
1. Layers: **crust (SiAl/SiMa) - mantle - core (NiFe)**; outer core liquid, inner core solid.
2. Discontinuities top to bottom: **Conrad (in crust), Moho (crust-mantle), Repetti (in mantle), Gutenberg (mantle-outer core), Lehmann (outer-inner core)** - 'Come Make Good Lunch'.
3. Continental crust is lighter and thicker; oceanic crust is denser basalt.

example.q: The Gutenberg discontinuity separates which two layers of the Earth?
example.solution: The **mantle from the outer core** (about 2,900 km deep). Moho separates crust from mantle; Lehmann divides the two cores.

patterns.name: Seismic waves and earthquake vocabulary
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which wave cannot pass through liquid', focus vs epicentre, Richter vs Mercalli, seismograph, 'Ring of Fire'.
patterns.logic:
1. Waves: **P** fastest (passes all matter), **S** stops in liquids (proves the outer core is molten), **L** surface waves - slowest, most destructive.
2. **Focus** = origin inside; **epicentre** = surface point above it; waves recorded on a **seismograph**.
3. Magnitude = **Richter** scale; damage intensity = **Mercalli** scale. About 80% of earthquakes strike the **Circum-Pacific 'Ring of Fire'**.

example.q: The point inside the Earth where an earthquake originates is called the:
example.solution: **Focus (hypocentre)**. The point on the surface directly above it - where the shock is felt first and strongest - is the **epicentre**.

patterns.name: Rock families and metamorphic pairs
patterns.howToSpot: 'Marble is formed from', 'fossils are found in which rock', 'which is an igneous rock', classify a list of rocks.
patterns.logic:
1. Three families: **igneous** (cooled magma - granite, basalt), **sedimentary** (strata, the only rocks with fossils - limestone, sandstone, shale, coal), **metamorphic** (changed by heat-pressure).
2. Metamorphic pairs: limestone-marble, sandstone-quartzite, shale-slate, granite-gneiss.
3. Igneous rocks are the oldest 'primary' rocks; sedimentary rocks cover most of the land surface and hold coal and oil.

example.q: Slate, used for roofing, is a metamorphic rock formed from which parent rock?
example.solution: **Shale**. The other classic pairs: limestone-marble, sandstone-quartzite, granite-gneiss.

patterns.name: Volcanoes: activity, shape and famous names
patterns.howToSpot: 'India's only active volcano', 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean', shield vs composite volcano, Krakatoa/Vesuvius events.
patterns.logic:
1. Activity: **active** (Barren Island - India's only one; Stromboli; Etna; Vesuvius), **dormant** (Fuji), **extinct**.
2. Shape: **shield** (broad, fluid lava - Mauna Loa, Hawaii), **composite/strato** (steep, alternating layers - Fuji, Vesuvius), **caldera** (collapsed crater).
3. Volcanoes cluster in the **Ring of Fire** and along mid-ocean ridges; Krakatoa (Indonesia, 1883) is the classic explosive eruption.

example.q: Stromboli, often called the 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean', is a/an:
example.solution: **Active volcano** (in the Aeolian islands, Italy) - its regular night glow guided sailors for centuries.

patterns.name: Mountain and landform types
patterns.howToSpot: 'Young fold mountains are', 'rift valley is formed by', block mountains with faults, highest/largest plateaus.
patterns.logic:
1. **Fold** mountains - squeezed crust; young folds (Himalaya, Alps, Andes, Rockies) are the highest, old folds (Aravallis, Urals) are worn down.
2. **Block** mountains - raised fault blocks (Vosges, Black Forest); **rift valleys** - sunken blocks between faults (Rhine valley, East African rift).
3. **Plateau** = raised flatland (Tibet highest and largest); **plain** = low, flat, fertile, most populated.

example.q: The Rhine valley and the East African rifts are examples of:
example.solution: **Rift valleys** - long, narrow sunken blocks (graben) formed where land has dropped between parallel faults.

subtopics.title: Atmosphere, pressure belts, planetary and local winds
subtopics.concept:
### Composition (dry air by volume)
**Nitrogen ~78%**, **Oxygen ~21%**, **Argon ~0.93%**, **Carbon dioxide ~0.04%**, plus traces of neon, helium, ozone and variable water vapour.

### Layers of the atmosphere (from the surface up)
| Layer | Key facts |
|---|---|
| **Troposphere** | All **weather**; temperature falls about **6.5 °C per km** (normal lapse rate); about 8 km thick at poles, 18 km at equator; ends at the **tropopause** |
| **Stratosphere** | Contains the **ozone layer** (absorbs UV); calm air — preferred by **jet aircraft** |
| **Mesosphere** | **Coldest** layer; **meteors burn** here |
| **Thermosphere** | Contains the **ionosphere**, which **reflects radio waves**; auroras |
| **Exosphere** | Outermost, very thin air merging into space |

### Pressure belts and planetary winds
- Equatorial low (**doldrums**), subtropical highs (**horse latitudes**, ~30°), sub-polar lows (~60°), polar highs.
- **Trade winds** blow from subtropical highs to the equator (NE trades in the north, SE trades in the south).
- **Westerlies** blow from subtropical highs towards 60°; in the Southern Hemisphere they are called the **Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties and Shrieking Sixties**.
- **Coriolis force** deflects winds to the **right in the Northern** and **left in the Southern** Hemisphere (**Ferrel's law**).

### Local winds (very common PYQ)
| Wind | Region | Nature |
|---|---|---|
| **Chinook** | Rocky Mountains (USA–Canada) | Warm, dry; '**snow eater**' |
| **Foehn** | **Alps** (Switzerland) | Warm, dry; helps grapes ripen |
| **Sirocco** | Sahara → Italy, Mediterranean | Hot, dusty; '**blood rain**' |
| **Harmattan** | West Africa | Dry, dusty from the Sahara; called '**The Doctor**' |
| **Mistral** | Rhône valley, **France** | Cold, northerly |
| **Bora** | Adriatic coast | Cold, dry |
| **Khamsin** | **Egypt** | Hot, dusty |
| **Santa Ana** | Southern California | Hot, dry; spreads wildfires |
| **Brickfielder** | Australia (Victoria) | Hot, dry |
| **Loo** | North India | Hot, dry summer wind |

### Tropical cyclones — same storm, different names
**Hurricane** (Atlantic, Caribbean), **Typhoon** (north-west Pacific — China, Japan, Philippines), **Cyclone** (Indian Ocean), **Willy-willy** (older term for north-west Australia). A **tornado** is a small, violent land funnel, most frequent in the USA.

tricks.title: Layer order: 'The Strong Man Throws Eggs'

example.q: In which layer do meteors burn up?
example.solution: The mesosphere.

tricks.title: Local wind by country
tricks.body: Chinook–**USA/Canada**, Foehn–**Alps**, Sirocco–**Sahara→Italy**, Harmattan–**West Africa**, Mistral–**France**, Khamsin–**Egypt**, Santa Ana–**California**, Loo–**India**.

mistakes: Placing the ozone layer in the troposphere — it is in the stratosphere.
Calling the Harmattan a cold wind — it is dry and dusty; 'Doctor' because it relieves humid heat.
Saying Coriolis deflects to the left in the Northern Hemisphere — it is to the right.
subtopics.notes:
### What the atmosphere is made of
The atmosphere is the blanket of air held by gravity. Dry air by volume: **Nitrogen 78%**, **Oxygen 21%**, **Argon 0.93%**, **Carbon dioxide about 0.04%**, plus traces of neon, helium and **ozone**, and variable **water vapour and dust**. Water vapour and dust matter because clouds and rain form around them; CO2 matters because it traps heat (the **greenhouse effect**, together with methane and water vapour).

### The five layers - bottom to top
| Layer | Height (about) | Remember for |
|---|---|---|
| **Troposphere** | 8 km (poles) - 18 km (equator) | **All weather** occurs here; temperature falls **6.5 degrees C per km** (normal lapse rate); ends at the tropopause |
| **Stratosphere** | up to 50 km | **Ozone layer (15-35 km)** absorbs ultraviolet rays, so temperature rises with height; calm air - **jet aircraft fly here** |
| **Mesosphere** | up to 80-85 km | **Meteors burn up** here; **coldest layer** (about -90 degrees C) |
| **Thermosphere (Ionosphere)** | up to about 600 km | Electrically charged ions **reflect radio waves**; **auroras** (northern/southern lights); the ISS orbits at about 400 km |
| **Exosphere** | beyond | Outermost; air so thin that satellites pass through almost freely |

**Ozone (O3)** shields life from UV-B rays. Its thinning - the 'ozone hole' over **Antarctica** (first reported in 1985) - was caused mainly by **CFCs**; the **Montreal Protocol (1987)** phases them out, and the layer is slowly healing.

### Pressure belts and planetary winds
Air pressure falls with height but also varies with temperature. Four classic belts circle the Earth:
- **Equatorial low (Doldrums, 0-5 degrees)** - rising warm air, daily convectional rain, calm winds.
- **Subtropical high (Horse latitudes, 25-35 degrees)** - sinking air, calm, dry - the great deserts (Sahara, Thar, Australian) lie under it.
- **Subpolar low (about 60 degrees)** - stormy convergence zone.
- **Polar high** - cold, dense, sinking air.
The equatorial low and polar high have a **thermal** origin (temperature); the other two are **dynamic** (formed by descending/converging air).

Winds blow from **high to low** pressure and are bent by the Earth's rotation (right in the Northern Hemisphere, left in the Southern - the Coriolis effect). Three planetary belts: **Trade winds** (from subtropical highs to the equatorial low - north-east trades in the north, south-east trades in the south; steady and reliable), **Westerlies** (35-60 degrees; in the southern ocean they are the **Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties and Shrieking Sixties**, because there is little land to break them), and **Polar easterlies**. The trade winds of the two hemispheres meet along the **ITCZ** (Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone), which follows the Sun and gives the **monsoon** its seasonal reversal.

### Cyclones, local winds and rainfall types
**Tropical cyclones** are violent spirals born over warm seas between 5-20 degrees latitude. Names by region: **Hurricane** (Atlantic, Caribbean, east Pacific), **Typhoon** (China Sea, north-west Pacific), **Willy-Willy** (Australia), simply **Cyclone** (Indian Ocean). A **tornado** is a much smaller funnel vortex of the American midwest ('twister') - not a tropical cyclone. **Temperate (frontal) cyclones** form along fronts in mid-latitudes; the winter **western disturbances** that rain on north India are weak temperate systems.

Local winds worth a flashcard set - **Hot:** Loo (India-Pakistan), Sirocco (Sahara to Italy, carrying red dust - 'blood rain'), Khamsin (Egypt), Brickfielder (Australia), Zonda (Argentina), **Chinook** ('snow eater' on the east slope of the Rockies) and **Foehn** (Alps - melts snow, ripens grapes). **Cold:** Mistral (Rhone valley, France), Bora (Adriatic), Blizzard (snow-laden, polar), Buran (Russia), Pampero (pampas of Argentina), **Harmattan** (dry, dusty West African wind, called 'The Doctor'). Rain falls in three ways - **convectional** (daily afternoon showers of the equator), **orographic/relief** (windward slopes - Cherrapunji's rain) and **cyclonic/frontal**.

### Quick revision
- Air: N2 78, O2 21, Ar 0.93, CO2 0.04 (%); weather = troposphere; ozone = stratosphere; meteors burn = mesosphere; aurora/radio = ionosphere.
- Lapse rate 6.5 degrees C per km; jets fly in the stratosphere; coldest layer = mesosphere.
- Belts: Doldrums (equatorial low), Horse latitudes (subtropical high); trades, westerlies, polar easterlies.
- Roaring Forties etc. = southern westerlies; ITCZ moves with the Sun - monsoon link.
- Hurricane (Atlantic), Typhoon (NW Pacific), Willy-Willy (Australia); tornado is different.
- Chinook snow-eater, Foehn Alps, Mistral France, Harmattan West Africa 'Doctor'.

patterns.name: Composition and layers of the atmosphere
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which gas is most abundant', 'weather occurs in which layer', lapse-rate and layer-feature questions, aurora/ozone/meteor placement.
patterns.logic:
1. Dry air: **N2 78%, O2 21%, Ar 0.93%, CO2 0.04%**; water vapour and dust vary.
2. Layers bottom-up: **Troposphere** (all weather; lapse rate 6.5 C/km) - **Stratosphere** (ozone 15-35 km; jets) - **Mesosphere** (meteors burn; coldest) - **Thermosphere/Ionosphere** (aurora, radio reflection, ISS) - **Exosphere**.
3. Place each fact in its layer before looking at options.

example.q: The normal lapse rate - the fall of temperature with height in the troposphere - is about:
example.solution: **6.5 degrees C per km.** All weather is confined to the troposphere, whose top (tropopause) lies at 8 km over the poles and 18 km over the equator.

patterns.name: Ozone layer and environmental facts
patterns.howToSpot: 'Ozone hole appears over', 'Montreal Protocol', 'which gas absorbs ultraviolet rays', CFC questions.
patterns.logic:
1. **Ozone (O3)** in the stratosphere (15-35 km) absorbs harmful UV rays; it is a trace gas, not a layer of pure gas.
2. The 'ozone hole' appears seasonally over **Antarctica** (first reported 1985); the main culprits are **CFCs**.
3. The **Montreal Protocol (1987)** phased out CFCs, and the layer is slowly recovering.

example.q: The ozone hole was first detected over which region?
example.solution: **Antarctica** - a springtime thinning of the ozone layer, blamed mainly on man-made **CFCs** and checked by the Montreal Protocol of 1987.

patterns.name: Pressure belts and planetary winds
patterns.howToSpot: 'Doldrums lie at', 'Roaring Forties are', 'trade winds blow from', horse latitudes, ITCZ, wind deflection.
patterns.logic:
1. Belts: equatorial **low (Doldrums)**, subtropical **high (Horse latitudes)**, subpolar low, polar high; deserts sit under the subtropical highs.
2. Winds: **trades** (NE in the north, SE in the south, towards the equator), **westerlies** (35-60 degrees; southern ones = Roaring Forties, Furious Fifties, Shrieking Sixties), polar easterlies.
3. Rotation deflects winds right in the Northern and left in the Southern Hemisphere; the **ITCZ** (where trades meet) follows the Sun - the basis of the monsoon.

example.q: The 'Roaring Forties' are strong winds found in the:
example.solution: **Southern Hemisphere westerlies** (40-50 degrees S) - so named because almost unbroken ocean lets them blow at full strength.

patterns.name: Cyclones: names by region and types
patterns.howToSpot: 'Typhoons occur in', 'willy-willy is a cyclone of', hurricane/typhoon/cyclone matching, tornado identification, temperate cyclones.
patterns.logic:
1. Tropical cyclone names: **Hurricane** - Atlantic/Caribbean and east Pacific; **Typhoon** - China Sea/north-west Pacific; **Willy-Willy** - Australia; **Cyclone** - Indian Ocean.
2. A **tornado** is a small, violent funnel (USA midwest, 'twister') - not a tropical cyclone.
3. **Temperate (frontal) cyclones** form in mid-latitudes; India's winter 'western disturbances' are weak temperate systems that rain on Punjab-Haryana.

example.q: Tropical cyclones of the China Sea and the north-west Pacific are called:
example.solution: **Typhoons.** The same storms are hurricanes in the Atlantic and willy-willies off Australia.

patterns.name: Local winds: name ↔ region ↔ character
patterns.howToSpot: 'Chinook is a wind of', 'Harmattan is called the Doctor', 'which wind melts snow', hot/cold local wind matching.
patterns.logic:
1. Warm: **Loo** (N. India summer), **Sirocco** (Sahara to Italy, red dust), Khamsin (Egypt), **Chinook** ('snow eater', east of the Rockies), **Foehn** (Alps - melts snow, ripens vines), Brickfielder (Australia), Zonda (Argentina).
2. Cold: **Mistral** (Rhone valley, France), **Bora** (Adriatic), **Blizzard** (snow-laden), Buran (Russia), Pampero (pampas), **Harmattan** (dry, dusty West Africa - 'The Doctor').
3. Match region first, then hot/cold character; distractors usually come from the other hemisphere.

example.q: The warm, dry **Foehn** wind that melts snow on the lee side of mountains blows over which region?
example.solution: The **Alps** (Europe). Its North American equivalent on the east slope of the Rockies is the **Chinook**, the 'snow eater'.

subtopics.title: Oceans, currents, straits and canals
subtopics.concept:
### Oceans
| Ocean | Key facts |
|---|---|
| **Pacific** | **Largest and deepest**; **Mariana Trench** (Challenger Deep, about 11 km) |
| **Atlantic** | Second largest, **S-shaped**; busiest shipping; Mid-Atlantic Ridge |
| **Indian** | Only ocean **named after a country** |
| **Southern** | Surrounds Antarctica |
| **Arctic** | **Smallest and shallowest** |

### Ocean currents
| Warm currents | Cold currents |
|---|---|
| **Gulf Stream** (N Atlantic, warms NW Europe) | **Labrador** (off Canada) |
| **Kuroshio** (Japan) | **Oyashio** (Japan) |
| Brazil, **Agulhas** (SE Africa), East Australian | **Humboldt / Peru** (W South America) |
| North Atlantic Drift | **Benguela** (SW Africa), **Canary**, **California**, West Australian, Falkland |

- **Cold currents** off **western coasts** of continents in the subtropics create **deserts**: Humboldt → **Atacama**, Benguela → **Namib**, California → Sonoran/Mojave, West Australian → Great Australian desert.
- Meeting of warm and cold currents creates rich **fishing grounds**: **Grand Banks** (Newfoundland) where the **Gulf Stream meets the Labrador current**; Kuroshio–Oyashio off Japan.
- **El Niño** is the periodic warming of the eastern Pacific off Peru; it tends to weaken the Indian monsoon.

### Straits and canals
| Strait | Connects / separates |
|---|---|
| **Palk** | India – Sri Lanka |
| **Gibraltar** | **Spain – Morocco**; Mediterranean ↔ Atlantic |
| **Bering** | **Russia (Asia) – Alaska (N America)**; near the Date Line |
| **Malacca** | Malay Peninsula – Sumatra; Andaman Sea ↔ South China Sea |
| **Hormuz** | **Iran – Oman**; Persian Gulf ↔ Gulf of Oman (oil route) |
| **Bab-el-Mandeb** | Yemen – Djibouti; **Red Sea ↔ Gulf of Aden** |
| **Bosphorus** | Istanbul; **Black Sea ↔ Sea of Marmara** |
| **Dover** | England – France |
| **Magellan** | South American mainland – Tierra del Fuego |
| **Sunda** | Java – Sumatra |
| **Cook** | North and South islands of New Zealand |
| **Bass** | Australia – Tasmania |

Canals: **Suez** (1869) — Mediterranean ↔ Red Sea (Egypt); **Panama** (1914) — Atlantic ↔ Pacific; **Kiel** — North Sea ↔ Baltic (Germany).

tricks.title: Cold current → desert pairs
tricks.body: **H**umboldt–**A**tacama, **B**enguela–**N**amib, **C**alifornia–**S**onoran. West coasts + cold current = dry air = desert.

example.q: Which cold current is responsible for the Namib desert?
example.solution: The Benguela current.

tricks.title: Strait → two countries
tricks.body: Gibraltar = Spain|Morocco; Hormuz = Iran|Oman; Bering = Russia|USA; Malacca = Malaysia|Indonesia; Palk = India|Sri Lanka; Dover = UK|France.

mistakes: Calling the Gulf Stream a cold current — it is warm.
Saying the Atlantic is the deepest ocean — the Pacific (Mariana Trench) is.
Linking the Suez Canal to the Atlantic — it joins the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.
subtopics.notes:
### The five oceans
Oceans cover about **71%** of the Earth's surface and hold about 97% of its water.
| Ocean | Remember for |
|---|---|
| **Pacific** | **Largest and deepest**; **Mariana Trench** (Challenger Deep, about 11 km) - the deepest point on Earth; ringed by the Ring of Fire |
| **Atlantic** | Second largest, **S-shaped**; busiest shipping ocean; **Mid-Atlantic Ridge** runs down its middle |
| **Indian** | The only ocean **named after a country**; the warmest |
| **Southern** | Surrounds **Antarctica** (recognised separately in 2000) |
| **Arctic** | **Smallest and shallowest**; partly frozen; the Bering Strait joins it to the Pacific |

**Salinity** (saltiness) averages **35 parts per thousand (3.5%)**. It is higher where evaporation beats river inflow - the **Red Sea** is the saltiest sea (about 41 per thousand) - and lower where big rivers dilute the water, as in the **Baltic Sea**, the least salty. The saltiest water body on Earth is the landlocked **Dead Sea** lake, so dense that swimmers float.

### Ocean currents - rivers in the sea
Currents are huge loops driven by **prevailing winds and the Earth's rotation**. **Warm currents** flow from the equator towards the poles; **cold currents** return polar water.
- Warm: **Gulf Stream** + **North Atlantic Drift** (keep the ports of western Europe ice-free), **Kuroshio** (Japan), **Brazilian**, **Agulhas** (south-east Africa).
- Cold: **Labrador** (Newfoundland), **Canary** (north-west Africa), **Benguela** (south-west Africa), **Humboldt/Peru** (western South America), **Oyashio** (Kamchatka).
Where a warm and a cold current meet, plankton multiply and fish gather: the **Grand Banks** (Gulf Stream x Labrador, off Newfoundland, famous for cod and fog) and the **Dogger Bank** (North Sea). Cold currents running along desert coasts dry the air - they help create the **Atacama** (Humboldt) and **Namib/Kalahari margin** (Benguela) deserts. The calm, weed-choked middle of the North Atlantic gyre is the **Sargasso Sea**, the 'sea without shores'. An **El Nino** is an abnormal warming of the Peruvian coast (the Humboldt current weakens), linked with weak Indian monsoons; **La Nina** is its opposite, linked with strong monsoons.

### Straits and canals - the chokepoints
| Waterway | Connects / separates | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Suez Canal (1869)** | Mediterranean - Red Sea | Sea-level canal (no locks), about 193 km; separates **Africa from Asia** |
| **Panama Canal (1914)** | Atlantic - Pacific | Lock canal, about 82 km; separates **North from South America** |
| **Strait of Gibraltar** | Atlantic - Mediterranean | Between **Spain and Morocco** |
| **Bosphorus + Dardanelles** | Black Sea - Sea of Marmara - Aegean | Both in **Turkey**; Istanbul straddles the Bosphorus |
| **Strait of Hormuz** | Persian Gulf - Gulf of Oman | Between **Iran and Oman/UAE**; the world's key oil route |
| **Bab-el-Mandeb** | Red Sea - Gulf of Aden | Djibouti-Yemen corner; the Suez route's gate |
| **Strait of Malacca** | Indian Ocean (Andaman Sea) - South China Sea | Between **Malaysia and Sumatra (Indonesia)**; busiest Asian route |
| **Palk Strait** | India - Sri Lanka | With the Gulf of Mannar to its south |
| **Bering Strait** | Arctic - Pacific; **Asia - North America** | Between **Russia and Alaska (USA)**; the two Diomede islands face each other |
| **Drake Passage** | South America - Antarctica | The roughest waters |
| **Strait of Dover** | UK - France | Narrowest part of the Channel |

### Coral reefs and tides
**Coral polyps** are tiny animals; their limestone skeletons build reefs. They need **warm (over about 20 degrees C), clean, shallow salt water**, so reefs grow in tropical seas and die near muddy river mouths. The **Great Barrier Reef** (north-east Australia, Coral Sea) is the **largest living structure on Earth**. Reef shapes: fringing, barrier and **atoll** (a ring around a sunken volcano). Warming seas cause **coral bleaching**.
**Tides** are the twice-daily rise and fall of the sea, caused mainly by the **Moon's pull** (assisted by the Sun). At **new moon and full moon** (Sun, Moon, Earth in line) the pulls add up - high-range **spring tides**; at the quarter moons the pulls work at right angles - low-range **neap tides**. The **Bay of Fundy** (Canada) records the world's highest tidal range.

### Quick revision
- Pacific largest + Mariana Trench deepest; Atlantic S-shaped + busiest; Indian = country's name; Arctic smallest.
- Average salinity 35 per thousand; Red Sea saltiest sea, Baltic least, Dead Sea saltiest lake.
- Warm: Gulf Stream, Kuroshio, Agulhas; Cold: Labrador, Canary, Benguela, Humboldt (El Nino).
- Fishing grounds form where warm meets cold: Grand Banks, Dogger Bank; Sargasso Sea = 'sea without shores'.
- Suez 1869 (Africa-Asia, no locks), Panama 1914 (locks, N-S America); Gibraltar = Spain-Morocco; Hormuz = oil gate.
- Spring tide at new/full moon, neap at quarters; Bay of Fundy = highest range.

patterns.name: Ocean superlatives and the five oceans
patterns.howToSpot: 'Largest/deepest ocean', 'which ocean is named after a country', 'Mariana Trench lies in', ordering of the five oceans.
patterns.logic:
1. Size order: **Pacific > Atlantic > Indian > Southern > Arctic**; Pacific is also the deepest and holds most of the world's water.
2. Deepest point: **Mariana Trench (Challenger Deep, about 11 km)** in the **Pacific**.
3. The **Indian Ocean** is the only one named after a country; the **Southern Ocean** (2000) encircles Antarctica; the **Arctic** is the smallest and shallowest.

example.q: Which is the deepest ocean of the world?
example.solution: The **Pacific Ocean** - it holds the Mariana Trench, whose **Challenger Deep (about 11 km)** is the deepest known point on Earth.

patterns.name: Ocean currents ↔ nature ↔ effects
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which is a warm current', 'Gulf Stream affects the climate of', 'which current makes a desert', fog and fishing grounds.
patterns.logic:
1. Warm: **Gulf Stream + North Atlantic Drift** (keeps west Europe warm), Kuroshio, Brazilian, Agulhas, Eskimo-free East Australian.
2. Cold: **Labrador** (icebergs, fog off Newfoundland), **Canary** (Canary Islands), **Benguela** (Namib), **Humboldt/Peru** (Atacama, rich anchovies, El Nino connection), Oyashio.
3. Where a warm and cold current meet (Grand Banks, Dogger Bank) plankton blooms - hence the world's best **fishing grounds**; cold currents running along coasts make the **Atacama and Namib deserts**.

example.q: The warm North Atlantic Drift keeps the climate of which region unusually mild for its latitude?
example.solution: **Western Europe (British Isles, Norway's coast)** - it is the eastward continuation of the Gulf Stream; the Labrador cold current meets the Gulf Stream near Newfoundland, making the Grand Banks foggy and rich in fish.

patterns.name: Straits: two water bodies and two lands
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which strait separates X from Y', 'which strait connects the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden', match-the-column on straits.
patterns.logic:
1. **Palk Strait** - India-Sri Lanka (Gulf of Mannar south of it); **Bering Strait** - Russia-Alaska (Arctic-Pacific); **Drake Passage** - South America-Antarctica (roughest).
2. **Hormuz** - Persian Gulf (oil route); **Bab-el-Mandeb** - Red Sea-Gulf of Aden; **Malacca** - Andaman Sea-China Sea (longest, busiest); **Bosphorus + Dardanelles** - Black Sea-Mediterranean through Turkey.
3. **Gibraltar** - Spain (Europe)-Morocco (Africa), Atlantic-Mediterranean. Learn each strait as four boxes: two lands, two waters.

example.q: The Strait of Hormuz connects the Persian Gulf with the:
example.solution: **Gulf of Oman (Arabian Sea)** - the world's most important oil-shipping bottleneck between Iran and Oman/UAE.

patterns.name: Canals and man-made sea links
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which canal joins the Mediterranean and the Red Sea', 'Suez/Panama canal connects', locks, year of opening.
patterns.logic:
1. **Suez Canal (1869)** - Mediterranean-Red Sea; in **Egypt**; sea-level, **no locks**, about 193 km; Europe-Asia trade shortcut.
2. **Panama Canal (1914)** - Atlantic-Pacific; in **Panama**; a **lock** canal about 82 km; joins Colon to Panama City.
3. 'Kiel Canal' joins the North Sea and the Baltic (Germany) - a favourite third option.

example.q: The Suez Canal, opened in 1869, lies in which country and connects which two seas?
example.solution: It lies in **Egypt** and joins the **Mediterranean Sea with the Red Sea**, cutting the Europe-Asia voyage by about 7,000 km; being sea-level, it has no locks.

patterns.name: Salinity, coral reefs and tides
patterns.howToSpot: 'Highest salinity is in', 'coral reefs need', 'Great Barrier Reef lies off', spring vs neap tides, Bay of Fundy.
patterns.logic:
1. Average ocean salinity **35 per mille**; highest in the **Red Sea (about 41)** - hot, dry, no fresh rivers; lowest in the **Baltic** (many rivers, low evaporation). **Dead Sea** = saltiest lake, bodies float.
2. Corals need **clean, shallow, warm (over 20 C), salt water**; types: fringing, barrier, **atoll** (ring); **Great Barrier Reef** off Queensland (Australia) is the largest living structure; warm-water stress causes **bleaching**.
3. Tides: **spring tides** - new/full moon (highest); **neap tides** - first/third quarter (lowest); **Bay of Fundy** (Canada) = highest tidal range.

example.q: Which water body has the highest average salinity among the seas?
example.solution: The **Red Sea** (about 41 per mille) - high evaporation, low rainfall and hardly any fresh-water rivers. The Baltic has the lowest.

subtopics.title: Continents, superlatives, grasslands and tribes
subtopics.concept:
### Continents — superlatives
| Feature | Answer |
|---|---|
| Largest / smallest continent | **Asia** / **Australia** |
| Highest peak | **Mount Everest**, 8,848.86 m (Nepal–China, 2020 joint measurement) |
| Highest peak of Africa / S America / N America / Europe / Antarctica / Australia | **Kilimanjaro** / **Aconcagua** / **Denali** / **Elbrus** / **Vinson Massif** / **Kosciuszko** |
| Longest mountain range | **Andes** |
| Longest river | **Nile** (Africa) |
| Largest river by volume | **Amazon** (South America) |
| Largest hot desert | **Sahara**; largest desert overall is **Antarctica** |
| Driest place | **Atacama** (Chile) |
| Largest lake | **Caspian Sea** |
| Largest freshwater lake (area) | **Lake Superior** (USA–Canada) |
| Deepest (and oldest) lake | **Lake Baikal** (Russia) |
| Highest navigable lake | **Lake Titicaca** (Peru–Bolivia) |
| Lowest point on land | **Dead Sea** shore (Jordan–Israel) |
| Largest island | **Greenland** |
| Largest / smallest country | **Russia** / **Vatican City** |

### Temperate grasslands and savannas
| Name | Region |
|---|---|
| **Prairies** | North America |
| **Pampas** | Argentina |
| **Veld** | South Africa |
| **Steppes** | Eurasia (Ukraine–Kazakhstan) |
| **Downs** | Australia |
| **Canterbury** | New Zealand |
| **Llanos** | Venezuela–Colombia (tropical) |
| **Campos** | Brazil (tropical) |
| **Savanna** | Africa (tropical) |

### Tribes and their homelands
**Masai** — Kenya/Tanzania; **Bedouin** — Arabian and Saharan deserts; **Inuit (Eskimo)** — Arctic Canada, Greenland, Alaska; **Pygmies** — Congo basin; **San (Bushmen)** — Kalahari; **Maori** — New Zealand; **Aborigines** — Australia; **Sami (Lapps)** — northern Scandinavia; **Ainu** — Japan.

example.q: The temperate grasslands of South Africa are called?
example.solution: Veld.

tricks.title: Lake superlatives
tricks.body: **Caspian** largest (salt), **Superior** largest freshwater, **Baikal** deepest, **Titicaca** highest navigable, **Dead Sea** lowest.

mistakes: Calling the Sahara the largest desert overall — Antarctica is; Sahara is the largest hot desert.
Saying the Amazon is the longest river — it carries the most water; the Nile is the longest.
Placing the Veld in South America — it is in South Africa.
subtopics.notes:
### Seven continents, one size ladder
There are **seven continents**. By area, from largest to smallest: **Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe, Australia**. Asia holds about 30% of the world's land and most of its people; **Australia** is the smallest and flattest, and with no land borders it is a 'continental country'.

### Superlatives the exam repeats
| Feature | Answer |
|---|---|
| Highest peak | **Mount Everest 8,848.86 m** (Nepal-China border; jointly re-measured in 2020) |
| Highest by continent | Kilimanjaro (Africa), **Aconcagua** (S. America), **Denali** (N. America), **Elbrus** (Europe), Vinson Massif (Antarctica), Kosciuszko (Australia) |
| Longest mountain range | **The Andes** (about 7,000 km) - longest in the world; the Himalaya-Karakoram has the highest peaks |
| Longest rivers | **Nile** (about 6,650 km) usually quoted as longest; **Amazon** carries the largest volume of water |
| Largest desert | **Sahara** (hot desert, North Africa); the coldest desert is Antarctica itself |
| Largest island | **Greenland** (the largest island - Australia, being a continent, does not count) |
| Largest lake | **Caspian Sea** (salt lake); largest **freshwater** lake by area - **Lake Superior** (N. America) |
| Deepest lake | **Lake Baikal** (Russia) - deepest freshwater lake |
| Highest waterfall | **Angel Falls** (Venezuela, about 979 m) |
| Lowest land point | **Dead Sea shore** (about 430 m below sea level) |
| Highest plateau | **Tibet**; the meeting of ranges at the **Pamir Knot** is the 'roof of the world' |

### Continent by continent - the one-liners
- **Asia:** Everest; the Dead Sea depression; **Baikal** (deepest) and the **Caspian** (largest lake); the **Yangtze**; the **Sundarbans**, the world's largest delta; Mesopotamia (Tigris-Euphrates); the equator crosses its islands (Indonesia).
- **Africa:** the 'Dark Continent'; **54 countries**, the most; the **Sahara**; the **Nile** (White and Blue Niles meet at **Khartoum**); **Kilimanjaro**; **Lake Victoria**; the **Great Rift Valley**; it straddles the equator.
- **North America:** **Denali**; the **Rockies** and Appalachians; the **Mississippi-Missouri** system; the five **Great Lakes** (Superior, Michigan - the only one wholly in the USA - Huron, Erie, Ontario) with **Niagara Falls** between Erie and Ontario; the **Grand Canyon** on the Colorado; **Death Valley**; **Greenland**, the largest island.
- **South America:** the **Andes**; **Aconcagua**; the **Amazon** and its rainforest, the world's largest; **Angel Falls**; the **Atacama**, driest non-polar desert; the **Pampas**; **Lake Titicaca**, the highest large navigable lake; La Paz, the world's highest capital city.
- **Europe:** **Vatican City**, the smallest country; the **Alps**; **Elbrus**; the **Volga** (longest) and the **Danube** (most countries crossed); Norwegian **fjords**; no true desert.
- **Australia/Oceania:** the **Great Barrier Reef**; **Uluru (Ayers Rock)** monolith; **Mount Kosciuszko**; the **Murray-Darling** rivers; kangaroo and emu; the **Great Dividing Range**.
- **Antarctica:** coldest, driest, windiest (-89.2 degrees C at Vostok); about **98% ice sheet**; **no permanent population** - only research stations (India: Dakshin Gangotri, **Maitri**, **Bharati**); highest peak **Vinson Massif**; run under the **Antarctic Treaty (1959)**.

### Grasslands of the world - by name
| Type | Region | Name |
|---|---|---|
| Tropical | East Africa | **Savanna** |
| Tropical | Venezuela (Orinoco) | **Llanos** |
| Tropical | Brazil | **Campos** |
| Temperate | North America | **Prairies** (wheat basket) |
| Temperate | Russia-Central Asia | **Steppes** |
| Temperate | Argentina-Uruguay | **Pampas** (cattle, wheat) |
| Temperate | South Africa | **Veld** |
| Temperate | Australia | **Downs** |
| Temperate | New Zealand | **Canterbury** |

### Peoples of the world - tribe by region
**Pygmies** - Congo rainforest; **Bushmen (San)** - Kalahari; **Masai** - Kenya-Tanzania savanna; **Bedouins** - Arabia; **Tuaregs and Berbers** - Sahara; **Inuit (Eskimo)** - Arctic Canada, Greenland, Alaska; **Lapps (Sami)** - northern Scandinavia; **Kirghiz** - Central Asian steppes; **Aborigines** - Australia; **Red Indians (Amerindians)** - the Americas; **Fuegians** - Tierra del Fuego; **Ainus** - Hokkaido, Japan; **Gonds and Bhils** - central India.

### Quick revision
- Size: Asia > Africa > N. America > S. America > Antarctica > Europe > Australia.
- Everest 8,848.86 m (2020); Kilimanjaro-Africa, Aconcagua-SA, Denali-NA, Elbrus-Europe, Vinson-Antarctica.
- Nile longest, Amazon biggest volume; Sahara largest hot desert; Greenland largest island.
- Caspian largest lake, Superior largest freshwater, Baikal deepest; Angel Falls highest waterfall.
- Grasslands: Prairies-Steppes-Pampas-Veld-Downs; tropical Savanna-Llanos-Campos.
- Antarctica: coldest/driest/windiest, no permanent people; Indian stations Maitri and Bharati.

patterns.name: World superlatives: mountains, rivers, deserts, lakes, falls
patterns.howToSpot: 'Longest river', 'highest peak of each continent', 'largest island/lake', 'lowest point of land', 'highest waterfall'.
patterns.logic:
1. Peaks: Everest (Asia, 8,848.86 m), Kilimanjaro (Africa), Denali (N. America), Aconcagua (S. America), Elbrus (Europe), Vinson (Antarctica), Kosciuszko (Australia).
2. Rivers: **Nile longest (about 6,650 km)**, **Amazon largest by volume**; Deserts: **Sahara** largest hot desert; Lakes: **Caspian** largest, **Superior** largest freshwater, **Baikal** deepest, **Titicaca** highest navigable.
3. Extremes: **Angel Falls** highest (979 m), **Dead Sea** lowest land (about 430 m below sea level), **Greenland** largest island, **Andes** longest mountains, **Tibet** highest plateau.

example.q: Which is the largest island in the world?
example.solution: **Greenland** - about 21.6 lakh sq km; Australia is larger but counted as a continent, not an island.

patterns.name: Continent ↔ one-line identity
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which continent has no desert', 'most countries', 'longest river of each continent', 'fjords', continent lists.
patterns.logic:
1. **Africa** - 54 countries, the most; the Nile (longest river) and the Sahara; the Great Rift Valley; Blue and White Nile meet at Khartoum; Lake Victoria largest African lake.
2. **Asia** - largest continent; Lake Baikal (deepest), Caspian (largest lake), Yangtze (longest Asian river), Sundarbans; Mesopotamia ('cradle of civilisation').
3. **Europe** - no hot desert; fjords in Norway; Vatican smallest country; Volga longest river of Europe; Danube passes through the most countries (10+). **Australia** - smallest continent; Great Barrier Reef, Uluru, Murray-Darling. **Antarctica** - coldest (-89.2 C at Vostok), no permanent population, 98% under ice; Antarctic Treaty 1959.

example.q: Which continent has the largest number of independent countries?
example.solution: **Africa** - 54 countries. (Asia has about 48; Europe about 44.)

patterns.name: Grasslands by continent
patterns.howToSpot: 'Prairies are in', 'Savanna is a grassland of', 'which grassland is in South America', match-the-column on temperate/tropical grasslands.
patterns.logic:
1. Tropical: **Savanna** (Africa), **Llanos** (Venezuela), **Campos** (Brazil), 'Downs' (Australia).
2. Temperate: **Prairies** (North America), **Steppes** (Eurasia/Russia), **Pampas** (Argentina - wheat, beef), **Veld** (South Africa), **Downs** (Australia), Canterbury (New Zealand).
3. Fix the four classic ones - Prairies, Pampas, Steppes, Veld - and the rest follow by elimination.

example.q: The temperate grasslands of South Africa are called:
example.solution: The **Veld**. (Prairies - North America, Steppes - Eurasia, Pampas - Argentina, Downs - Australia.)

patterns.name: Tribes and their native regions
patterns.howToSpot: 'Bushmen live in', 'which tribe of the Congo forest', 'Masai are cattle herders of', match-the-column on tribes.
patterns.logic:
1. Africa: **Pygmies** - Congo basin; **Bushmen** - Kalahari; **Masai** - East Africa (Kenya-Tanzania); **Bedouins** - Arabia; **Tuaregs/Berbers** - Sahara.
2. Cold lands: **Inuit (Eskimos)** - Arctic Canada/Greenland/Alaska; **Lapps** - northern Scandinavia; **Kirghiz** - Central Asian steppes.
3. Others: **Aborigines** - Australia; **Red Indians** - North America; **Fuegians** - Tierra del Fuego; **Ainus** - Japan.

example.q: The Bushmen, famous hunters of the Kalahari desert, belong to which continent?
example.solution: **Africa** - the Kalahari lies in Botswana/Namibia. Pygmies are their Congo-basin counterparts.

patterns.name: Antarctica and the polar regions
patterns.howToSpot: 'Antarctica is covered by', 'which country has research stations in Antarctica', 'Antarctic Treaty year', Arctic vs Antarctica.
patterns.logic:
1. Antarctica: about **98% under an ice sheet**, average 2,000 m thick; coldest place **Vostok, about -89.2 C**; highest peak **Vinson Massif**; **no permanent human population**.
2. The **Antarctic Treaty (1959, in force 1961)** reserves the continent for peaceful scientific use; India runs the **Dakshin Gangotri, Maitri and Bharati** stations.
3. Arctic vs Antarctica: the Arctic is an **ocean** ringed by land (Inuit live there); Antarctica is **land** ringed by ocean.

example.q: The Antarctic Treaty, which keeps the continent for peaceful scientific activity, was signed in:
example.solution: **1959** (in force 1961). India's Antarctic stations are **Dakshin Gangotri, Maitri and Bharati**.
