tricks.title: Sun pair
tricks.body: **Rising** Sun = **Japan** (east of Asia, first sunrise); **Midnight** Sun = **Norway** (Arctic summer).

tricks.title: Line → neighbours: 'Radcliffe-Rift, McMahon-Mountains, Durand-Afghan'
tricks.body: Radcliffe partitioned **India–Pakistan**, McMahon runs along the Himalayas with **China**, Durand divides **Pakistan–Afghanistan**.

example.q: The Durand Line separates which countries?
example.solution: Pakistan and Afghanistan.

mistakes: Assigning the Durand Line to India–Afghanistan — today it is the Pakistan–Afghanistan border.
Confusing Finland (thousand lakes) with Norway (midnight sun).
Placing the 38th parallel between the two Vietnams — it divides the Koreas; Vietnam was split at the 17th.
subtopics.notes:
### Country nicknames - the classic table
| Nickname | Country / region |
|---|---|
| Land of the **Rising Sun** | **Japan** (easternmost, so it sees the Sun first) |
| Land of the **Midnight Sun** | **Norway** (summer sun never sets in the far north) |
| Land of a **Thousand Lakes** | **Finland** |
| Land of the **White Elephant** | **Thailand** |
| Land of the **Thunder Dragon** | **Bhutan** (Druk Yul) |
| **Sugar Bowl** of the world | **Cuba** |
| **Emerald Isle** | **Ireland** |
| **Gift of the Nile** | **Egypt** (Herodotus's phrase) |
| **Playground of Europe** | **Switzerland** |
| **Roof of the World** | **Pamir Knot** (Tibet region) |
| **Land of the Maple Leaf** | **Canada** |
| Land of the **Morning Calm** | **Korea** |
| **Land of Fire and Ice** | **Iceland** (volcanoes under glaciers) |
| Land of the **Long White Cloud** | **New Zealand** (Aotearoa) |
| Land of the **Golden Fleece** | **Australia** (wool) |
| **Dark Continent** | **Africa** |

City nicknames: **Big Apple** - New York; **Eternal City** and **City of Seven Hills** - Rome; **City of Light** - Paris; **Windy City** - Chicago; **City of Canals** - Venice; **Forbidden City** - the imperial palace in Beijing (Lhasa too was long closed to outsiders); **Golden City** - Johannesburg; **City of the Golden Gate** - San Francisco.

### Boundary lines - who drew what where
| Line | Between | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Durand Line (1893)** | **Pakistan - Afghanistan** | Drawn by Sir Mortimer Durand with the Afghan ruler |
| **Radcliffe Line (1947)** | **India - Pakistan** | Demarcated at Partition by Sir Cyril Radcliffe |
| **McMahon Line (1914)** | **India - China (Tibet region)** | Named after Sir Henry McMahon, Simla talks |
| **38th Parallel** | **North Korea - South Korea** | Fixed in 1945; the DMZ lies near it |
| **49th Parallel** | **USA - Canada** | Long, straight surveyed border |
| **17th Parallel** | Former **North - South Vietnam** | Historical line of the 1954 Geneva accord |
| **Maginot Line** | **France - Germany** | French fortification belt built in the 1930s |
| **Hindenburg Line** | German defensive line in the **First World War** | Often asked with the Western Front |
| **Oder-Neisse Line** | **Germany - Poland** | Set after the Second World War |
| **Mannerheim Line** | **Finland - Russia** | Finnish defence line of the Winter War |

In a 'which line divides A and B' question, first match the pair (India-Pakistan = Radcliffe; Pakistan-Afghanistan = Durand; India-China = McMahon; Korea = 38th; US-Canada = 49th), because the same question is asked with the options reshuffled.

### Old names and new names
Many exam questions give the **old name** and ask for the modern one (or the reverse):
- **Ceylon to Sri Lanka (1972)**; **Burma to Myanmar (1989)**; **Siam to Thailand**; **Persia to Iran (1935)**; **Abyssinia to Ethiopia**; **Formosa to Taiwan**; **Kampuchea - Cambodia**; **Gold Coast to Ghana (1957)**; **Rhodesia to Zimbabwe (1980)**; **Nyasaland to Malawi**; **Dutch East Indies to Indonesia**; **East Pakistan to Bangladesh (1971)**.
- Cities: **Constantinople to Istanbul** (Turkey); **Peking to Beijing** (China); **Rangoon to Yangon** (Myanmar); **Saigon to Ho Chi Minh City** (Vietnam); **Batavia to Jakarta** (Indonesia); **Leningrad to St Petersburg** (Russia); **Bombay to Mumbai, Madras to Chennai, Calcutta to Kolkata** (India).

### Capitals and the rivers they stand on
| Capital | River | Capital | River |
|---|---|---|---|
| London | Thames | Cairo | Nile |
| Paris | Seine | Baghdad | **Tigris** |
| Rome | Tiber | Khartoum | White and Blue Nile meet |
| Moscow | Moskva | Delhi | Yamuna |
| Berlin | Spree | Dhaka | Buriganga |
| Vienna, Budapest, Belgrade | Danube | Bangkok | Chao Phraya |
| Warsaw | Vistula | Hanoi | Red River |
| Prague | Vltava | Seoul | Han |
| Ottawa | Ottawa River | Tokyo | Sumida |
| Washington | Potomac | Lisbon | Tagus |

Baghdad on the **Tigris** (not the Euphrates) and Khartoum at the **Nile confluence** are the two favourites. Danube capitals in order downstream: Vienna - Budapest - Belgrade.

### Quick revision
- Rising Sun Japan, Midnight Sun Norway, Thunder Dragon Bhutan, White Elephant Thailand, Emerald Isle Ireland, Sugar Bowl Cuba.
- Boundary pairs: Radcliffe India-Pak, Durand Pak-Afghan, McMahon India-China, 38th Korea, 49th US-Canada.
- Old-to-new: Ceylon-Sri Lanka, Burma-Myanmar, Siam-Thailand, Persia-Iran, Constantinople-Istanbul, Rangoon-Yangon, Peking-Beijing.
- Baghdad-Tigris, Khartoum-Nile confluence, Cairo-Nile, Paris-Seine, Danube trio Vienna-Budapest-Belgrade.

patterns.name: Country nicknames
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which country is called the Land of the Rising Sun', 'Land of Thousand Lakes', 'Land of White Elephant', nickname matching.
patterns.logic:
1. Sun/light: **Rising Sun - Japan**, **Midnight Sun - Norway**, Morning Calm - Korea, Land of the Maple Leaf - Canada.
2. Water/nature: **Thousand Lakes - Finland**, Fire and Ice - Iceland, Long White Cloud (Aotearoa) - New Zealand, **Thunder Dragon - Bhutan**, Emerald Isle - Ireland.
3. Symbols/food: **White Elephant - Thailand**, Sugar Bowl - Cuba, Gift of the Nile - Egypt, Playground of Europe - Switzerland, Land of the Golden Fleece - Australia.

example.q: Which country is called the 'Land of the Thunder Dragon'?
example.solution: **Bhutan** - 'Druk Yul' in Dzongkha, the land of the thunder dragon; its flag also bears the dragon.

patterns.name: City nicknames
patterns.howToSpot: 'Big Apple', 'City of Seven Hills', 'Eternal City', 'City of Light', which-city-is-called questions.
patterns.logic:
1. **New York - Big Apple**; **Rome - Eternal City / City of Seven Hills**; **Paris - City of Light**; **Chicago - Windy City**.
2. **Venice - City of Canals**; **Beijing - the Forbidden City** (after the imperial palace); **Johannesburg - City of Gold** (gold mines); San Francisco - Golden Gate City.
3. Distractors usually swap a European city pair - Rome and Paris are the classic confusion.

example.q: Which city is known as the 'Big Apple'?
example.solution: **New York**. Rome is the 'Eternal City' and the 'City of Seven Hills'; Paris the 'City of Light'.

patterns.name: Boundary lines and borders
patterns.howToSpot: 'Durand/Radcliffe/McMahon line separates', '38th parallel divides', '49th parallel', 'Maginot line', match-the-column.
patterns.logic:
1. India: **Durand Line (1893)** - Pakistan-Afghanistan; **Radcliffe Line (1947)** - India-Pakistan; **McMahon Line (1914)** - India-China (Arunachal side).
2. Koreas - **38th Parallel**; USA-Canada - **49th Parallel**; North-South Vietnam - **17th Parallel**.
3. Fortification lines: **Maginot** - France-Germany (WW2 defences); **Hindenburg** - German WW1 line; **Oder-Neisse** - Germany-Poland; **Mannerheim** - Finland-Russia.

example.q: The McMahon Line is the boundary between:
example.solution: **India and China** - drawn at the 1914 Simla Convention, running along the eastern (Arunachal Pradesh) sector; the Durand Line separates Pakistan and Afghanistan.

patterns.name: Old names → new names
patterns.howToSpot: 'Siam is the old name of', 'Ceylon is now', 'Constantinople', old-new matching for countries and cities.
patterns.logic:
1. Countries: **Ceylon - Sri Lanka (1972)**, Burma - Myanmar (1989), Siam - Thailand, Persia - Iran (1935), Abyssinia - Ethiopia, Formosa - Taiwan, Gold Coast - Ghana (1957), Rhodesia - Zimbabwe (1980), East Pakistan - Bangladesh (1971).
2. Cities: **Constantinople - Istanbul**, Peking - Beijing, Rangoon - Yangon, Saigon - Ho Chi Minh City, Batavia - Jakarta, Leningrad - St Petersburg.
3. Indian cities: Bombay-Mumbai, Madras-Chennai, Calcutta-Kolkata - but exam questions normally ask the foreign ones.

example.q: 'Siam' was the former name of which country?
example.solution: **Thailand.** Ceylon became Sri Lanka; Burma became Myanmar; Persia became Iran.

patterns.name: Capitals on rivers
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which capital stands on the Danube', 'Baghdad is on which river', 'Paris is on the Seine', capital-river matching.
patterns.logic:
1. Own small rivers: **London - Thames, Paris - Seine, Rome - Tiber, Moscow - Moskva, Berlin - Spree, Warsaw - Vistula, Prague - Vltava, Ottawa - Ottawa, Washington - Potomac.**
2. Big rivers: **Cairo - Nile, Baghdad - Tigris, Khartoum - confluence of Blue and White Nile, Delhi - Yamuna, Dhaka - Buriganga, Bangkok - Chao Phraya, Hanoi - Red River, Seoul - Han.**
3. **Danube** flows through Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade - four capitals on one river.

example.q: Which river flows through Vienna, Budapest and Belgrade - three European capitals?
example.solution: The **Danube** - it also passes through Bratislava, making four capitals on one river; the Rhine does not touch any capital.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Largest/hottest/brightest/smallest planet', 'Earth's twin', 'red planet', 'which planet has rings', 'largest satellite of a planet'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Hold one anchor fact per planet and eliminate: Mercury smallest, Venus hottest-brightest-retrograde and 'Earth's twin', Mars red with Olympus Mons, Jupiter largest with Ganymede, Saturn ringed and least dense. Superlative questions are almost always about Jupiter, Saturn, Venus or Mars.

example.q: Which is the largest planet of the solar system?
example.solution: **Jupiter** - followed by Saturn, Uranus, Neptune; its Great Red Spot is a giant storm and Ganymede is its (and the solar system's) largest satellite.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Two places 15/30/60 degrees apart, what is the time difference?', 'IST is ahead of GMT by', 'crossing the IDL from east to west', '1 degree of longitude equals'.
pyqPatterns.approach: One formula does it all: 1 degree = 4 minutes, so degrees x 4 = minutes of time; east is ahead, west behind. IST = GMT + 5 h 30 min (82.5 E). Across the International Date Line: travelling eastwards, lose a day; westwards, add a day.

example.q: What is the time difference between two places 15 degrees of longitude apart?
example.solution: **1 hour** (15 x 4 minutes = 60 minutes); the eastern place is ahead of the western one.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which discontinuity separates crust and mantle', 'which wave cannot pass through liquid', 'focus/epicentre', 'rocks are classified into', 'marble is formed from'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Two ladders solve this block. Layers top to bottom with their discontinuities - Conrad, Moho (crust-mantle), Repetti, Gutenberg (mantle-core), Lehmann - and waves P (fastest), S (blocked by liquid), L (most destructive). Rocks: igneous-sedimentary-metamorphic with the four pairs limestone-marble, sandstone-quartzite, shale-slate, granite-gneiss.

example.q: Which discontinuity separates the mantle from the core?
example.solution: The **Gutenberg discontinuity** (about 2,900 km deep). Moho separates the crust from the mantle.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Weather occurs in which layer', 'aurora/ozone/meteors belong to which layer', 'composition of air', 'lapse rate', 'jet planes fly in which layer'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Place every fact in its layer: troposphere - weather, water vapour, 6.5 C/km lapse; stratosphere - ozone, calm jet routes; mesosphere - meteors burn, coldest; thermosphere/ionosphere - aurora, radio waves, ISS; exosphere - outermost. Composition: N2 78, O2 21, Ar 0.93, CO2 0.04 per cent.

example.q: In which layer of the atmosphere do jet aircraft normally fly to avoid weather disturbances?
example.solution: The **stratosphere** - calm, cloudless air above the tropopause, with the ozone layer (15-35 km) inside it.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Loo/Chinook/Foehn/Mistral/Sirocco/Harmattan is a wind of which region', 'which wind is called the snow eater/Doctor', warm-vs-cold wind matching.
pyqPatterns.approach: Learn two buckets per hemisphere pair. Warm: Loo (N. India), Chinook ('snow eater', east of Rockies), Foehn (Alps), Sirocco (Sahara to Italy, red dust), Khamsin (Egypt). Cold: Mistral (Rhone, France), Bora (Adriatic), Blizzard, Buran (Russia), Pampero (Argentina), Harmattan (West Africa, dry dust, 'The Doctor'). Region first, then hot/cold.

example.q: The Chinook, known as the 'snow eater', blows down which mountains?
example.solution: The **Rockies** of North America - its warm dry air melts snow on the eastern (lee) slopes overnight; the Foehn is its Alpine counterpart.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which strait separates X from Y', 'which canal connects two seas', 'Hormuz/Bab-el-Mandeb/Malacca', 'Suez vs Panama canal'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Fix each strait as four boxes - two lands, two waters: Gibraltar (Spain-Morocco, Atlantic-Mediterranean), Hormuz (Persian Gulf-Oman Gulf), Bab-el-Mandeb (Red Sea-Gulf of Aden), Malacca (Andaman-China seas), Bering (Russia-Alaska), Palk (India-Sri Lanka). Canals: Suez (Egypt, 1869, sea-level, no locks, Mediterranean-Red Sea) vs Panama (1914, locks, Atlantic-Pacific).

example.q: The Suez Canal connects the Mediterranean Sea with the —
example.solution: **Red Sea.** It runs sea-level through Egypt (opened 1869) with no locks; the Panama Canal (1914) is a lock canal joining the Atlantic and Pacific.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which is a warm/cold current', 'which current keeps west Europe warm', 'which current causes fog/fishing grounds', 'current responsible for a coastal desert'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Warm set: Gulf Stream + North Atlantic Drift (west Europe mild), Kuroshio, Brazilian, Agulhas. Cold set: Labrador (Newfoundland fog and icebergs), Canary, Benguela (Namib), Humboldt/Peru (Atacama, anchovies, El Nino), Oyashio. Where warm meets cold - Grand Banks, Dogger Bank - plankton blooms make the great fishing grounds.

example.q: Which cold current flowing along the western coast of South America is linked with the Atacama desert and the anchovy fishery?
example.solution: The **Humboldt (Peru) current** - cold water chills the coast (Atacama's dryness) yet upwells nutrients for anchovies; its warm-phase reversal is El Nino.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Prairies/Pampas/Steppes/Veld are grasslands of', 'Pygmies/Bushmen/Masai/Inuit live in', 'Land of Rising Sun/Thousand Lakes/White Elephant', old-name-new-name questions.
pyqPatterns.approach: Three mini-tables. Grasslands: Prairies-North America, Pampas-Argentina, Steppes-Eurasia, Veld-South Africa, Downs-Australia, Savanna/Llanos/Campos-tropical. Tribes: Pygmies-Congo, Bushmen-Kalahari, Masai-East Africa, Inuit-Arctic, Lapps-Scandinavia, Bedouins-Arabia, Aborigines-Australia. Names: Ceylon-Sri Lanka, Siam-Thailand, Persia-Iran, Constantinople-Istanbul, Gold Coast-Ghana.

example.q: The temperate grasslands of Eurasia are called —
example.solution: The **Steppes** (Ukraine to Central Asia). Prairies - North America, Pampas - Argentina, Veld - South Africa.

solvedExamples.q: Which planet is known as the 'Earth's twin' and is also the hottest planet of the solar system?
solvedExamples.solution: **Venus** has nearly the same size and mass as the Earth (hence 'twin'). Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere causes a runaway greenhouse effect, making it hotter than Mercury even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Greenhouse beats distance: Venus > Mercury in temperature.

solvedExamples.q: If it is 10:00 a.m. at a place on 15°W, what is the local time at a place on 75°E?
solvedExamples.solution: Longitude difference = 15 + 75 = **90°** (they are on opposite sides of Greenwich, so add). Time difference = 90 × 4 = 360 min = **6 hours**. The eastern place is ahead: 10:00 a.m. + 6 h = **4:00 p.m.**
solvedExamples.shortcut: Opposite sides → add degrees; divide by 15 for hours: 90/15 = 6 h.

solvedExamples.q: The Chinook, a warm and dry wind known as the 'snow eater', blows along the eastern slopes of the:
solvedExamples.solution: The **Chinook** descends the eastern (leeward) slopes of the **Rocky Mountains** in the USA and Canada. It warms by compression and melts snow quickly. The similar wind of the **Alps** is the **Foehn**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Chinook — a Native American name → North America → Rockies.

solvedExamples.q: The Strait of Hormuz connects which two water bodies?
options: Red Sea and Gulf of Aden
Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman
Black Sea and Sea of Marmara
solvedExamples.solution: The **Strait of Hormuz** lies between **Iran** and **Oman** and links the **Persian Gulf** to the **Gulf of Oman** (Arabian Sea) — a key oil route. Red Sea–Gulf of Aden is Bab-el-Mandeb; Black Sea–Marmara is Bosphorus; Mediterranean–Atlantic is Gibraltar.

practice.q: Which planet has the largest moon of the solar system, Ganymede?
practice.solution: **Ganymede**, a moon of **Jupiter**, is the largest natural satellite in the solar system — bigger than Mercury. Saturn's largest moon is Titan.

practice.q: On which date does the Northern Hemisphere experience its longest day?
practice.solution: On **21 June** (summer solstice) the Sun is overhead at the **Tropic of Cancer**, giving the Northern Hemisphere its longest day. 21 March and 23 September are equinoxes; 22 December is the winter solstice.

practice.q: A traveller crossing the International Date Line from east to west (for example, from the USA to Japan) will:
options: gain one day on the calendar
practice.solution: Moving **westward** across the IDL the calendar jumps **one day ahead** (e.g. Monday becomes Tuesday). Moving eastward the date goes back one day, so a day is repeated.
practice.shortcut: West-bound = skip ahead a day; East-bound = repeat a day.

practice.q: The boundary between the Earth's crust and the mantle is called the:
practice.solution: The **Mohorovičić (Moho) discontinuity** separates the crust from the mantle. Gutenberg separates mantle and core, Lehmann separates outer and inner core, and Conrad lies within the crust.
practice.shortcut: 'Come Make Good Lunch' — Moho is second.

practice.q: Marble is a metamorphic rock formed from which rock?
practice.solution: Heat and pressure recrystallise **limestone** (calcium carbonate) into **marble**. Sandstone becomes quartzite, shale becomes slate and granite becomes gneiss.

practice.q: Which seismic waves cannot travel through liquids?
practice.solution: **S-waves** (secondary, transverse) cannot pass through liquids. Their absence beyond about 103° from the epicentre (the S-wave shadow zone) showed that the **outer core is liquid**. P-waves pass through all states.

practice.q: The ozone layer, which absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation, lies mainly in the:
practice.solution: The **ozone layer** lies in the **stratosphere** (roughly 15–35 km). The troposphere has weather, the mesosphere burns meteors and the thermosphere contains the ionosphere.

practice.q: The dry, dusty Harmattan wind, locally called 'The Doctor', blows over:
practice.solution: The **Harmattan** blows from the Sahara over **West Africa** towards the Guinea coast. Its dryness brings relief from humid heat, hence 'The Doctor'. Egypt has the Khamsin, France the Mistral and California the Santa Ana.

practice.q: Tropical cyclones in the north-west Pacific Ocean (near China, Japan and the Philippines) are called:
practice.solution: They are **typhoons**. The same kind of storm is a **hurricane** in the Atlantic/Caribbean and a **cyclone** in the Indian Ocean. A tornado is a small land funnel, not a tropical cyclone.

practice.q: Which of the following is a cold ocean current?
practice.solution: The **Humboldt (Peru) Current** flows north along the west coast of South America and is **cold**; it supports rich fisheries and helps create the Atacama desert. Gulf Stream, Kuroshio and Agulhas are warm currents.
practice.shortcut: Cold currents hug western coasts in the subtropics.

practice.q: The Strait of Gibraltar separates which two countries?
practice.solution: The **Strait of Gibraltar** lies between **Spain** (Europe) and **Morocco** (Africa) and links the Mediterranean Sea with the Atlantic Ocean.

practice.q: Which is the deepest lake in the world?
practice.solution: **Lake Baikal** in Siberia (Russia) is the deepest and oldest lake and holds the largest volume of fresh water. The Caspian is the largest lake by area, Superior the largest freshwater lake by area and Titicaca the highest navigable lake.

practice.q: The temperate grasslands of Argentina are known as:
practice.solution: The **Pampas** are the temperate grasslands of **Argentina** (and Uruguay). Prairies are in North America, Steppes in Eurasia and Downs in Australia.

practice.q: Which country is known as the 'Land of the Midnight Sun'?
practice.solution: **Norway** lies largely north of the Arctic Circle, where the Sun stays visible at midnight in summer. Finland is the 'Land of Thousand Lakes' and Japan the 'Land of the Rising Sun'.

practice.q: The Durand Line forms the boundary between:
practice.solution: The **Durand Line** (1893, drawn by Sir Mortimer Durand) marks the **Pakistan–Afghanistan** border. India–China is the McMahon Line and India–Pakistan is the Radcliffe Line.

practice.q: Which planet of the solar system is the **hottest**?
practice.solution: **Venus** is the hottest planet because its thick carbon-dioxide atmosphere traps heat (runaway greenhouse effect); its surface is hotter even than Mercury's.
practice.shortcut: Closest to the Sun is Mercury; hottest is Venus.

practice.q: Which planet is called the **Morning Star** and the **Evening Star**?
practice.solution: **Venus** is the brightest planet and, seen near the horizon before sunrise or after sunset, was called the Morning and Evening Star.

practice.q: Which planet rotates on its axis from **east to west**, opposite to most planets?
practice.solution: **Venus** spins retrograde - east to west - so its Sun rises in the west. Uranus rolls on its side; the rest rotate west to east.

practice.q: Which planet is the **least dense** - so light it would float on water?
practice.solution: **Saturn's** density (about 0.7 g/cm3) is less than that of water. Its famous rings are pieces of ice and rock.

practice.q: The largest volcano of the solar system, **Olympus Mons**, is on which planet?
practice.solution: **Olympus Mons** rises on **Mars**, the 'Red Planet' (its colour comes from iron-oxide dust). Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.

practice.q: The average distance of the Moon from the Earth is about:
practice.solution: The Moon is about **3,84,000 km (3.84 lakh km)** away - light takes about 1.3 seconds to cross that gap.

practice.q: The Moon has practically no atmosphere because:
options: It is too far from the Sun
Its gravity is too weak to hold gases
practice.solution: The Moon's small mass gives it very weak gravity, so it cannot retain an atmosphere; hence the sky is black even in daytime and astronauts' footprints last for ages.

practice.q: Who was the first human being to walk on the Moon, in July 1969?
practice.solution: **Neil Armstrong** of Apollo 11 stepped onto the Moon on **20 July 1969** in the Sea of Tranquility; Buzz Aldrin followed, while Michael Collins orbited above.

practice.q: The Sun is vertically overhead the **Tropic of Cancer** on:
practice.solution: On **21 June**, the summer solstice, the Sun stands overhead the Tropic of Cancer and the Northern Hemisphere has its longest day.

practice.q: The Northern Hemisphere has its **shortest day** on:
practice.solution: On **22 December** (winter solstice) the Sun is overhead the Tropic of Capricorn; the north has its shortest day while the south enjoys midsummer.

practice.q: On the **equator**, the length of day and night through the year is:
practice.solution: The circle of illumination always bisects the equator, so days and nights stay roughly equal there; the contrast grows towards the poles.

practice.q: Day and night on the Earth are caused by:
practice.solution: The Earth's **rotation** on its axis once in about 24 hours turns one half towards the Sun (day) and the other away (night). Revolution causes the seasons.

practice.q: The exact time the Earth takes for one rotation with respect to the stars (the sidereal day) is:
practice.solution: The **sidereal day is 23 h 56 min 4 s**; the solar day we use averages 24 hours because the Earth also moves along its orbit.

practice.q: Earth is **nearest** to the Sun (perihelion) on:
practice.solution: **Perihelion falls on 3 January** (about 147 million km); aphelion, the farthest point (152 million km), comes on 4 July - so the north's winter happens near the nearest point.

practice.q: Indian Standard Time is ahead of GMT by:
practice.solution: IST is based on the 82.5 E meridian: 82.5 x 4 minutes = 330 minutes = **5 h 30 min** ahead of Greenwich.

practice.q: A traveller flying **east across the International Date Line** (from Asia towards America) must:
options: Add one day to the date
practice.solution: Across the IDL: going **east, lose a day**; going west (towards Asia), add a day. The line bends around islands so that no country is split into two dates.

practice.q: If the local time of place A (60 E) is 12 noon, what is the local time of place B (90 E)?
practice.solution: B lies 30 degrees **east** of A, so it is ahead: 30 x 4 min = 120 min = 2 hours. Local time at B = 12 noon + 2 h = **2 p.m.**

practice.q: Which layer of the Earth is made mainly of **nickel and iron**?
practice.solution: The **core (NiFe)** is iron-nickel; the outer core is liquid and the inner core solid. SiAl/SiMa describe the crust; the mantle is iron-magnesium silicate rock.

practice.q: The **Mohorovicic (Moho) discontinuity** separates:
practice.solution: **Moho = crust-mantle boundary** (1909). Gutenberg separates mantle and outer core; Conrad lies within the crust; Lehmann splits the two cores.

practice.q: Which of the following discontinuities lies **within the mantle**?
practice.solution: **Repetti** divides the upper and lower mantle. Conrad is inside the crust, Moho is crust-mantle, Gutenberg is mantle-core, Lehmann is between the cores.

practice.q: Earthquake waves are recorded by an instrument called the:
practice.solution: A **seismograph** records the shock waves. Richter and Mercalli are scales for magnitude and damage, not instruments.

practice.q: The energy released by an earthquake (its magnitude) is measured on the:
practice.solution: **Richter scale** = magnitude (energy). **Mercalli** = intensity of damage at a place. (Fujita rates tornadoes; Beaufort rates wind.)

practice.q: Which seismic waves are the **last to arrive** but cause the greatest destruction?
practice.solution: **L-waves** travel along the surface, arrive last, and shake buildings the most. P-waves are fastest; S-waves cannot cross liquids.

practice.q: About what share of the world's earthquakes occurs in the Circum-Pacific 'Ring of Fire'?
practice.solution: Roughly **80%** of the world's largest earthquakes - and most volcanoes - occur along the ring of subduction zones fringing the Pacific Ocean.

practice.q: Fossils of plants and animals are found only in which type of rock?
practice.solution: Only **sedimentary rocks** form in layers at the surface, where living remains can be buried; heat and pressure in other rocks destroy them.

practice.q: Quartzite is the metamorphic form of which rock?
practice.solution: **Sandstone - quartzite**. Limestone turns to marble, shale to slate, granite to gneiss.

practice.q: Granite and basalt are examples of which family of rocks?
practice.solution: **Igneous** rocks cool from magma or lava: granite (intrusive/plutonic, large crystals) and basalt (extrusive/volcanic, as on ocean floors and the Deccan).

practice.q: Which of the following is correctly matched?
practice.solution: **Slate comes from shale.** Marble is from limestone, gneiss from granite, quartzite from sandstone - the classic four pairs.

practice.q: **Barren Island**, India's only active volcano, lies in which water body?
practice.solution: **Barren Island** in the **Andaman Sea** (Andaman & Nicobar Islands) erupted again from 1991 onwards; nearby Narcondam is dormant.

practice.q: Which of these is a **shield volcano** with broad, gently sloping sides of fluid lava?
practice.solution: **Mauna Loa** (Hawaii) is the classic shield volcano. Fuji and Vesuvius are steep composite (strato) volcanoes built of alternating lava and ash.

practice.q: Mount Vesuvius, whose 79 AD eruption buried the Roman town of Pompeii, is located in:
practice.solution: **Vesuvius** stands near Naples, **Italy**; Pompeii lay under its ash. Etna (Sicily) and Stromboli are Italy's other famous volcanoes.

practice.q: The Himalayas, the Alps and the Andes are examples of:
practice.solution: They rose in the recent geological past where plates collided, so they are **young fold mountains** - the highest ranges on Earth. The Aravallis are old, worn folds.

practice.q: The Vosges and the Black Forest, raised between two faults, are examples of:
practice.solution: **Block mountains** (horsts) rise between parallel faults while rift valleys (graben) sink - as on either side of the Rhine rift.

practice.q: Which is the highest and largest plateau in the world?
practice.solution: The **Tibetan Plateau** ('the roof of the world', averaging over 4,500 m) is the highest and largest; the Pamir Knot, where ranges meet, lies at its western end.

practice.q: Which is the **most abundant gas** in the Earth's atmosphere?
practice.solution: **Nitrogen makes up about 78%** of dry air, oxygen about 21%, argon 0.93% and CO2 about 0.04%.

practice.q: Clouds, rain and storms - all weather - are confined to which layer?
practice.solution: Almost all water vapour lies in the **troposphere**, the lowest layer (8-18 km), so all weather happens there. Jet aircraft cruise above it, in the calm stratosphere.

practice.q: **Meteors** ('shooting stars') mostly burn up in which layer of the atmosphere?
practice.solution: The **mesosphere** (up to 80-85 km) is dense enough to burn incoming meteors by friction - and it is also the coldest layer (about -90 degrees C).

practice.q: The chemical formula of **ozone** is:
practice.solution: **Ozone is O3** - three oxygen atoms per molecule; it forms a shield in the stratosphere that absorbs ultraviolet rays.

practice.q: The **Montreal Protocol (1987)** is an international agreement to:
practice.solution: It phases out **CFCs** and related chemicals that destroy stratospheric ozone - the main cause of the ozone hole over Antarctica.

practice.q: Which atmospheric layer contains the ozone layer that absorbs ultraviolet radiation, and is therefore favoured by jet aircraft?
practice.solution: The **stratosphere** holds the ozone layer (15-35 km) and its calm, cloudless air suits long-haul flights.

practice.q: The equatorial belt of calm, rising air with daily convectional rains is called the:
practice.solution: The **Doldrums** (equatorial low, 0-5 degrees) are hot, humid and windless - sailing ships were often becalmed there. The subtropical high is the 'horse latitudes' belt.

practice.q: In the Northern Hemisphere, the **north-east trade winds** blow:
options: From the equatorial low towards the subtropical high
From west to east at 35-60 degrees
From the subtropical high towards the equatorial low
practice.solution: Trades flow out of the subtropical highs towards the Doldrums, deflected to become **north-east trades** in the north and **south-east trades** in the south.

practice.q: Winds are deflected to the **right of their path** in the Northern Hemisphere because of:
practice.solution: The **Coriolis effect** of the Earth's spin bends moving air right in the north and left in the south - shaping the trades, westerlies and cyclone spirals.

practice.q: A **tropical cyclone** occurring in the **Atlantic Ocean and Caribbean Sea** is called a:
practice.solution: Atlantic and east-Pacific storms are **hurricanes**; typhoon is the name in the north-west Pacific, willy-willy off Australia, and simply cyclone in the Indian Ocean.

practice.q: Which of the following is **NOT** a tropical cyclone?
practice.solution: A **tornado** is a narrow, violently rotating funnel typical of the American midwest - quite different from the broad warm-sea tropical cyclones.

practice.q: The winter rains of Punjab and Haryana, useful for the rabi crop, come from which weather system?
options: Tropical cyclones of the Bay of Bengal
practice.solution: **Western disturbances** are weak temperate (frontal) cyclones travelling from the Mediterranean region; they bring gentle winter rain to north-west India and snow to the hills.

practice.q: The warm, dry **'snow eater'** wind that blows down the eastern slopes of the Rockies in North America is the:
practice.solution: The **Chinook** melts the winter snow on the prairie side of the Rockies overnight. The Foehn is its Alpine counterpart.

practice.q: The **Mistral**, a cold, dry wind that chills the Rhone valley in winter, blows over:
practice.solution: The **Mistral** funnels down the Rhone valley in southern **France** towards the Mediterranean; the Bora is its cold counterpart on the Adriatic.

practice.q: The **Sirocco**, a hot wind that carries red dust from the Sahara and sometimes drops 'blood rain' on southern Europe, blows towards:
practice.solution: The **Sirocco** picks up heat and red dust crossing the Sahara and reaches Sicily and southern Italy. The Harmattan blows westward across West Africa.

practice.q: Which is the **largest ocean** in the world?
practice.solution: The **Pacific** is the largest and deepest ocean - it covers more area than all the land put together and holds the Mariana Trench.

practice.q: The Mariana Trench, the deepest known point of the oceans, lies in which ocean?
practice.solution: The **Mariana Trench** (Challenger Deep, about 11 km deep) lies in the western **Pacific**, near the Mariana Islands.

practice.q: Which ocean is the **only one named after a country**?
practice.solution: The **Indian Ocean** takes its name from India; it is the third largest and the warmest ocean.

practice.q: Which of these oceans was designated as a separate ocean most recently (in 2000), encircling Antarctica?
practice.solution: The **Southern Ocean** (Antarctic Ocean), circumscribing Antarctica, was recognised separately around **2000**; the Arctic remains the smallest ocean.

practice.q: Which of the following is a **warm ocean current**?
practice.solution: The **Gulf Stream** is a warm current of the Atlantic; Labrador, Canary and Benguela are all cold currents.

practice.q: Icebergs off Newfoundland and the fog over the Grand Banks are caused mainly by the meeting of:
practice.solution: The warm **Gulf Stream** meets the cold **Labrador current** off Newfoundland - fog and icebergs at the Grand Banks, plus rich fishing grounds where plankton thrives.

practice.q: The Atacama desert of South America owes its extreme dryness partly to the cold current flowing along its coast, called the:
practice.solution: The cold **Humboldt (Peru) current** cools the air, so little rain falls - making the Atacama. Its warm-water reversal is **El Nino**.

practice.q: The meeting of which two currents creates the rich Dogger Bank fishing ground of the North Sea?
options: North Atlantic Drift and Arctic cold current
practice.solution: Where the warm **North Atlantic Drift** meets cold Arctic water over the submerged moraine of the **Dogger Bank**, plankton abounds - hence herring and cod. Grand Banks is its Atlantic twin.

practice.q: The Bosphorus and the Dardanelles straits, connecting the Black Sea with the Mediterranean, lie in which country?
practice.solution: Both straits pass through **Turkey** - the Bosphorus at Istanbul (Sea of Marmara between them) and the Dardanelles towards the Aegean.

practice.q: Which strait separates India from Sri Lanka?
practice.solution: The **Palk Strait** lies between India (Tamil Nadu) and northern Sri Lanka; the Gulf of Mannar is south of it, with Adam's Bridge shoals in between.

practice.q: Which strait connects the **Red Sea** with the **Gulf of Aden** and lies between Yemen and Djibouti?
practice.solution: **Bab-el-Mandeb** ('Gate of Tears') guards the southern entrance to the Red Sea; Hormuz guards the Persian Gulf, Malacca the Andaman Sea-China Sea route.

practice.q: The Panama Canal connects the Atlantic Ocean with the:
practice.solution: The **Panama Canal** (opened 1914) cuts across the Isthmus of Panama between the Atlantic (Caribbean) and the **Pacific**; it is a lock canal.

practice.q: Which statement about the **Suez Canal** is correct?
options: It is in Panama and has six locks
It is in Egypt, is a sea-level canal without locks
It connects the Atlantic and Pacific oceans
practice.solution: The **Suez Canal** (1869, Egypt) runs sea-level from Port Said to Suez - **no locks** - and shortens the Europe-Asia route. Panama (1914) is the lock canal.

practice.q: The Kiel Canal connects the:
practice.solution: The **Kiel Canal** (Germany) joins the North Sea with the Baltic - a favourite distractor alongside Suez and Panama.

practice.q: The average salinity of ocean water is about:
practice.solution: Ocean water averages **35 per mille** (about 3.5% salt). The Red Sea reaches about 41; the Baltic may fall below 10.

practice.q: Corals cannot grow in which of the following conditions?
options: Deep water beyond the sunlight zone
Salt water of normal ocean salinity
practice.solution: Corals need **shallow, sunlit, clean, warm (over 20 C) salt water** - they live in symbiosis with algae that require light. Cold or muddy water kills them.

practice.q: The Great Barrier Reef, the largest coral reef of the world, lies off the coast of:
practice.solution: The **Great Barrier Reef** stretches about 2,000 km off Queensland, north-east **Australia** - the largest structure built by living organisms.

practice.q: **Spring tides**, the highest tides of the month, occur when:
options: The Moon is in its first quarter
The Sun, Moon and Earth are in a straight line (new or full moon)
The Moon is farthest from Earth
Strong winds pile water on the shore
practice.solution: At new and full moon the Sun's and Moon's pulls combine - spring tides; at the quarters (neap tides) they work at right angles and the range is least. The Bay of Fundy (Canada) has the world's highest tidal range.

practice.q: The longest river in the world is generally taken to be the:
practice.solution: The **Nile (about 6,650 km)** is the longest; the **Amazon** is the largest by volume of water. The Yangtze is the longest of Asia.

practice.q: The highest peak of **South America** is:
practice.solution: **Aconcagua** (Argentina, about 6,960 m) tops South America. Vinson - Antarctica, Denali - North America, Elbrus - Europe.

practice.q: Which is the **largest freshwater lake** in the world by area?
practice.solution: **Lake Superior** (USA-Canada) is the largest freshwater lake by area; Baikal is the **deepest**; the Caspian is the largest lake overall but salty.

practice.q: Angel Falls, the highest waterfall in the world, is located in:
practice.solution: **Angel Falls** (about 979 m) drops from the Auyan-tepui tableland in **Venezuela**.

practice.q: The lowest point of the Earth's land surface is:
practice.solution: The **Dead Sea** shore (Israel-Jordan) lies about **430 m below sea level** - the lowest land on Earth; its water is also the saltiest of lakes.

practice.q: Which continent is the largest by area?
practice.solution: **Asia** (about 44 million sq km) is the largest continent, with Africa second and Australia the smallest.

practice.q: The Blue Nile and the White Nile meet at:
practice.solution: They join at **Khartoum** (Sudan); the Blue Nile comes from Lake Tana in Ethiopia and carries most of the flood water.

practice.q: The fjord coast, carved by glaciers into deep sea inlets, is a typical feature of:
practice.solution: **Norway's** west coast is the classic land of **fjords**. The Volga is Europe's longest river; the Danube crosses the most countries.

practice.q: Which continent is **completely covered** in the statements: (1) no permanent population, (2) about 98% under an ice sheet?
practice.solution: **Antarctica** - scientists stay temporarily at research stations (India: Dakshin Gangotri, Maitri, Bharati); it is the coldest continent (Vostok, about -89 C).

practice.q: The Great Dividing Range and the Murray-Darling basin are features of:
practice.solution: The **Great Dividing Range** runs along Australia's east coast; the Murray-Darling is its chief river system. Uluru (Ayers Rock) lies in the centre.

practice.q: The temperate grasslands of **North America** are called:
practice.solution: **Prairies** - North America (wheat belt of Canada-USA). Pampas - Argentina; Steppes - Eurasia; Veld - South Africa.

practice.q: The **Pampas** grasslands, famous for wheat and beef cattle, lie in:
practice.solution: The **Pampas** of Argentina (and Uruguay) are among the world's great farm lands; Buenos Aires stands on their edge.

practice.q:
Match the grassland with its continent:
1. Llanos  2. Campos  3. Canterbury
(i) New Zealand (ii) Venezuela (iii) Brazil
practice.solution: **Llanos** - Venezuela (Orinoco), **Campos** - Brazil, **Canterbury** - New Zealand. All three are tropical (or southern temperate) grasslands.

practice.q: The **Inuit (Eskimos)** traditionally live in the:
options: Arctic regions of North America and Greenland
practice.solution: The **Inuit** are the indigenous people of the Arctic (Alaska, Canada, Greenland); the igloo and the kayak belong to their culture.

practice.q: The **Pygmies**, known as forest dwellers of short stature, live in the:
practice.solution: **Pygmies** - equatorial rainforests of the **Congo basin**. Bushmen - Kalahari; Masai - East African savanna; Tuaregs - Sahara.

practice.q: The **Lapps** (Sami), traditional reindeer herders, are found in:
practice.solution: The **Lapps** live in northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and the Kola peninsula; the Kirghiz are their steppe counterparts in Central Asia.

practice.q: Which country operates the Indian Antarctic research stations **Maitri** and **Bharati**?
practice.solution: **India** runs **Maitri** and **Bharati** (and the earlier, now-buried **Dakshin Gangotri**) - its first expedition reached Antarctica in 1981-82.

practice.q: The **Arctic** is different from Antarctica mainly because the Arctic is:
practice.solution: The Arctic is a **frozen ocean** ringed by the lands of North America, Europe and Asia; **Antarctica is land** ringed by the Southern Ocean.

practice.q: Which country is known as the 'Land of the Rising Sun'?
practice.solution: **Japan** - Nippon, 'origin of the sun', from its position east of the Asian mainland; its flag shows the sun disc.

practice.q: Which country is called the 'Land of a Thousand Lakes'?
practice.solution: **Finland** actually has about 1.88 lakh lakes; Canada has more lakes overall but Finland owns the nickname.

practice.q: The 'Land of the White Elephant' is:
practice.solution: **Thailand** - the white elephant was a royal symbol; it appears on the old flag. Bhutan is the 'Thunder Dragon' land.

practice.q: Which country is called the 'Land of the Midnight Sun' because summer days never fully end in its north?
practice.solution: **Norway** - north of the Arctic Circle the summer Sun never sets. Iceland is 'Fire and Ice'; Ireland the 'Emerald Isle'.

practice.q: Which city is called the 'Eternal City'?
practice.solution: **Rome** - also the 'City of Seven Hills'; Athens is the 'City of Violet Crowns' in older literature.

practice.q: The 'Windy City', famous for its strong lake breezes, is:
practice.solution: **Chicago**, on Lake Michigan, is the Windy City; New York is the Big Apple; San Francisco the Golden Gate City.

practice.q: Johannesburg, the centre of a great mining region, is called the:
practice.solution: **Johannesburg** grew on the Witwatersrand **gold** reefs. Kimberley, not Johannesburg, is linked with diamonds.

practice.q: The Radcliffe Line (1947) is the boundary between:
practice.solution: The **Radcliffe Line** was drawn in **1947** at Partition between India and (West) Pakistan; the Durand Line (1893) separates Pakistan and Afghanistan.

practice.q: The **38th Parallel** is associated with the boundary between:
practice.solution: The **38th Parallel** divides the two Koreas (armistice line, 1953). The 17th Parallel divided Vietnam; the 49th Parallel runs along much of the US-Canada border.

practice.q: The Maginot Line, a chain of concrete fortifications of the 1930s, was built by which country on its border with Germany?
practice.solution: **France** built the **Maginot Line**; German forces simply went around it in 1940. The Hindenburg Line was Germany's own WW1 defence line.

practice.q: Which of the following is correctly matched?
practice.solution: The **Oder-Neisse Line** runs along the Oder and Neisse rivers between Germany and Poland. Durand - Pak-Afghan; McMahon - India-China; Mannerheim - Finland-Russia.

practice.q: 'Ceylon' was the former name of which country?
practice.solution: **Ceylon** became **Sri Lanka** in **1972** when it became a republic; its capital is Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte (Colombo is the commercial hub).

practice.q: The city once called **Constantinople** is today known as:
practice.solution: **Constantinople** was renamed **Istanbul** (officially from 1930); Ankara is Turkey's capital. Peking-Beijing and Rangoon-Yangon are parallel cases.

practice.q: 'Gold Coast', a former British colony, is the old name of which country?
practice.solution: **Gold Coast** became **Ghana** at independence in **1957** - the first sub-Saharan colony to gain freedom. Rhodesia became Zimbabwe (1980).

practice.q: Baghdad, the capital of Iraq, stands on the bank of which river?
practice.solution: **Baghdad - Tigris.** Cairo stands on the Nile; Khartoum at the Blue-White Nile confluence.

practice.q: The capital of Egypt, Cairo, is situated on which river?
practice.solution: **Cairo - Nile**; Egypt itself is the 'Gift of the Nile'.

practice.q: Which of the following capital-river pairs is **wrong**?
practice.solution: **Berlin stands on the Spree** (and the Havel); the Rhine flows through Cologne and Rotterdam, not a capital.

practice.q: Bangkok, the capital of Thailand, lies on which river?
practice.solution: **Bangkok - Chao Phraya** ('River of Kings'). Hanoi - Red River; Dhaka - Buriganga; Yangon - Yangon river.

practice.q: Which single European river flows through the greatest number of capital cities?
practice.solution: The **Danube** passes through **Vienna (Austria), Bratislava (Slovakia), Budapest (Hungary) and Belgrade (Serbia)** - four capitals; the Volga is Europe's longest river but has no capital on it.
